title: BUG sample-weight ignored by `min_sample_leaf` in HGBDT
body:
Description
In the following course, we are using the weight of HGBDT to correct probability estimate. We know that it should be equivalent with a post-hoc correction. However, they are not equivalent for HGBDT while it works for logistic regression. In the past, we thought that it was due to the binning but it has been fixed (cf. #29641).
Potential cause (to be check further)
Splitter in sklearn/ensemble/_hist_gradient_boosting/splitting.pyx applies min_samples_leaf to histogram counts (n_samples_left / n_samples_right), not to the sum of sample weights (or hessians). Loss gradients/hessians (and bin edges after #29641) are weighted correctly.
Minimal reproducer
import numpy as np
from sklearn.base import clone
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.ensemble import HistGradientBoostingClassifier

X, y = make_classification(
    n_samples=1000,
    n_features=10,
    n_informative=5,
    n_redundant=0,
    weights=[0.75, 0.25],
    random_state=0,
)
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
sw = rng.randint(1, 4, size=len(y))
X_rep, y_rep = np.repeat(X, sw, axis=0), np.repeat(y, sw)


def max_raw_diff(min_samples_leaf):
    est = HistGradientBoostingClassifier(
        min_samples_leaf=min_samples_leaf,
        early_stopping=False,
        max_iter=50,
        random_state=0,
    )
    weighted = clone(est).fit(X, y, sample_weight=sw)
    repeated = clone(est).fit(X_rep, y_rep)
    return np.max(np.abs(weighted._raw_predict(X) - repeated._raw_predict(X)))


print(max_raw_diff(1))   # ~1e-8
print(max_raw_diff(20))  # ~2.4, unexpected
Observed on main (1.10.dev0):

min_samples_leaf=1: max |raw_pred| diff ≈ 4.6e-08
min_samples_leaf=20: max |raw_pred| diff ≈ 2.42

Expected behavior
Expect equivalence.
Notes

Documented limitation in test_sample_weight_effect (forces min_samples_leaf=1).
Related: #26128 (histogram counts vs weights). Not a regression of #29641; remaining gap after that fix.

title: BUG: Two ProgressBar on the same estimator raises a KeyErr

Introduce yourself
No response
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
Attaching two ProgressBar instances on the same estimator breaks on teardown when the second one tries to _run_queues.pop(context.root_uuid).
I see two options to address the issue:


Adding an attribute (maybe named _unique) to indicate that a callback can only have one instance attached to an estimator, and raising a ValueError if multiple are given to set_callbacks. This would also help the management of default callbacks in #34272 to ignore a default callback if one of the same unique callback was manually attached.


Constraining all callback classes to work when multiple instances are attached to the same estimator and fix ProgressBar to do so.


I have a preference for the first option, but I'd love to hear others' opinions.

title: PytestRemovedIn10Warning (pytest version 9.1.1.) with sklearn parametrize_with_checks
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
The recent pytest update (9.1.1) introduces a warning in our scikit-learn compatibility tests for our own encoders. Our encoder inherits from scikit-learn’s TransformerMixin and BaseEstimator, and we use sklearn.utils.estimator_checks.parametrize_with_checks to verify that the custom encoders are compatible with scikit-learn.
The warning originates from parametrize_with_checks, which essentially returns a pytest.mark.parametrize. It currently passes a generator to pytest.mark.parametrize. However, this is deprecated in current versions of pytest.
It would therefore be useful to review or update the parametrize_with_checks implementation so that it no longer relies on the deprecated generator behavior. This will allow us in the future to keep testing for scikit-learn compatibility.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
Run the following file using pytest's latest version (9.1.1):
import pytest
from sklearn.dummy import DummyRegressor
from sklearn.utils.estimator_checks import parametrize_with_checks


@parametrize_with_checks([DummyRegressor()])
def test(estimator, check):
    check(estimator)
This can be run from terminal with pytest name_of_file.py
Expected Results
The expected result is no warning about deprecation from pytest.
Actual Results

title: PRF: Over-subscription in pairwise_distances with `backend="threading"` + BLAS-pthreads
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

sklearn.metrics.pairwise_distances accepts a n_jobs parameters and uses joblib.Parallel(backend="threading", n_jobs=n_jobs) under-the-hood. But this parallelization happens on top on openBLAS parallelism, and can lead to what looks like over-subscription.
(but maybe it's not over-subscription, and something else, like cost of repeated small parallelized blas calls, etc. I haven't investigated)
Results from a small benchmark script shows that limiting blas to 1 thread helps scaling as n_jobs grows (and usually achieves best performance compared to n_jobs=1 with blas parallelism enabled):
--- n_samples=2000  n_features=200 ---
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=0:      33ms
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=1:      52ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=0:      66ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=1:      53ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=0:      76ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=1:      35ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=0:     102ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=1:      25ms

--- n_samples=4000  n_features=200 ---
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=0:     150ms
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=1:     226ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=0:     107ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=1:     102ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=0:     141ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=1:      75ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=0:     163ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=1:      70ms

--- n_samples=8000  n_features=200 ---
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=0:     547ms
  n_jobs=  1 | pin-blas=1:     864ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=0:     375ms
  n_jobs=  4 | pin-blas=1:     296ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=0:     356ms
  n_jobs=  8 | pin-blas=1:     217ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=0:     362ms
  n_jobs= 14 | pin-blas=1:     204ms

Results with 10 or 1000 features are similar, but for n_samples=2000, the n_jobs=1 pin-blas=0 variant wins.
The script:
Details
import argparse
from itertools import product
import time
from statistics import median

import numpy as np
import threadpoolctl

from sklearn.metrics import pairwise_distances


def bench_once(X, n_jobs, pin_blas):
    if pin_blas:
        with threadpoolctl.threadpool_limits(1, user_api="blas"):
            return pairwise_distances(X, X, n_jobs=n_jobs)
    return pairwise_distances(X, X, n_jobs=n_jobs)


def bench(X, n_jobs, pin_blas, reps):
    bench_once(X, n_jobs, pin_blas)  # warmup / compilation
    times = []
    for _ in range(reps):
        t0 = time.perf_counter()
        bench_once(X, n_jobs, pin_blas)
        times.append(time.perf_counter() - t0)
    return median(times)


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--n-samples", type=str, default="2000,4000,8000")
    parser.add_argument("--n-features", type=str, default="200")
    parser.add_argument("--n-jobs", type=str, default="1,4,8,14")
    parser.add_argument("--reps", type=int, default=30)
    args = parser.parse_args()

    n_samples_list = [int(v) for v in args.n_samples.split(",")]
    n_features_list = [int(v) for v in args.n_features.split(",")]
    n_jobs_list = [int(v) for v in args.n_jobs.split(",")]

    rng = np.random.RandomState(4872)

    for n_samples, n_features in product(n_samples_list, n_features_list):
        X = rng.rand(n_samples, n_features)
        print(f"\n--- n_samples={n_samples}  n_features={n_features} ---")

        for n_jobs in n_jobs_list:
            for pin_blas in [False, True]:
                t = bench(X, n_jobs, pin_blas, args.reps)
                print(f"  n_jobs={n_jobs:>3} | pin-blas={pin_blas:>1}: {t * 1000:7.0f}ms")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Note: the default metric is euclidean, but I think I observed similar behavior with cosine too. l1 doesn't call blas so it doesn't have the same issue.

title: BUG: Callback's _worker_connections cache grows too big
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
Using a ScoringMonitor in a lot of sub-estimators in sub-processes eventually raises an EOFError when trying to create the connection for the callback to communicate across processes.
After investigating with the help of an LLM, the suspect appears to be the _worker_connections. It stores new connections for each fit, but there is no mechanism to remove them from the cache. When persistent workers are used, like when using joblib's loky backend, the cache grows until the worker process hits its fd limit and the next time a connection is opened the handshake sequence breaks mid-flight, causing the EOFError.
The LLM's suggested fix is to have a max size for _worker_connections, using a least recently used eviction policy.
ping @jeremiedbb
Steps/Code to Reproduce
from sklearn.callback import ScoringMonitor
from sklearn.callback.tests._utils import (
    MaxIterEstimator,
    MetaEstimator,
)

for _ in range(120):
    callback = ScoringMonitor(scoring="r2")
    est = MaxIterEstimator(max_iter=2).set_callbacks(callback)
    meta_est = MetaEstimator(est, n_jobs=2, prefer="processes")

    meta_est.fit()

title: CI Align wheel workflow in `scikit-learn` and `scikit-learn-release` repos
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Looking at numpy approach, the idea would be to have scikit-learn wheels.yml be a "simplified" version of scikit-learn-release wheels.yml so that we can catch most wheels error in the scikit-learn repo. numpy went for one wheels build per platform with the minimal Python version.
There are at least to things:

 use cibuildwheel directly + remove the Docker set-up since the minimal Docker image is tested in scikit-learn-release. This would allow to get rid of the intermittent Docker on Windows GHA issue: #34569. There are other things to sync, like bash scripts and config (maybe it would be better if both repos use a pyroject.toml or a cibuildwheel.toml, rather than cibuildwheel.toml for scikit-learn-release and pyproject.toml)
 which wheels build do we want to run in scikit-learn and on which trigger. Do we want to do something like numpy, i.e. one wheels build per platform for the minimal Python version? Do we want to keep [cd build] to test wheels only on demand? See numpy PR for numpy and scipy PR for more details.

First item can be work on already. Second one may need a bit of discussion.
Caveat:

our lock-files setup gives us confidence that a new release of our dependencies will not break all PRs at once. What do we want to do about this if we start having wheels build on each PR push, hope that it doesn't happen this often? Last time it happened was with cython see #34525. In principle we should have caught it in the scipy-dev build and reported it earlier to cython but we didn't 🤷. An alternative is to have lock files in wheels build, see scikit-learn/scikit-learn-release#1, but that seems to be further away in the future IMO.

To think about for the future:

how do we make sure that both wheels.yml does not diverge too much. AFAICT numpy has not a ready-made solution but they introduced this check numpy/numpy#30166 to make sure that the pinned scipy-openblas version is the same in both repos.
automatic wheels failure issue creation, see scikit-learn/scikit-learn-release#6

title: Tests to detect overwritten attribute types in __init__
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the issue
The check_estimator utility in sklearn/tests/estimator_checks.py catches many violations of the class instantiation rules (https://scikit-learn.org/stable/developers/develop.html#instantiation).

There should be no logic, not even input validation, and the parameters should not be changed; which also means ideally they should not be mutable objects such as lists or dictionaries. If they’re mutable, they should be copied before being modified. The corresponding logic should be put where the parameters are used, typically in fit.

Certain edits to these rules pass the check_estimator associated tests but fail elsewhere, e.g., subtle changes to the object type. Below, I show examples where this violation from API compliance is caught indirectly in fit on edge cases but not under the test suite for API compliance.
Is it the intent of the testing suite to check or not to check the object type at instantiation?
Steps / code to reproduce
In sklearn/neural_network/_multilayer_perceptron.py lines 138 - 140:
self.loss = loss
- self.hidden_layer_sizes = hidden_layer_sizes
+ self.hidden_layer_sizes = np.asarray(hidden_layer_sizes)
self.shuffle = shuffle
This will result in TypeError for edge cases in python -m pytest sklearn/neural_network/tests but python -m pytest sklearn/utils/tests passes.
In sklearn/ensemble/_voting.py lines 348 - 350:
self.voting = voting
- self.weights = weights
+ self.weights = np.asarray(weights)
self.n_jobs = n_jobs
This will result in TypeError for edge cases in python -m pytest sklearn/ensemble/tests but python -m pytest sklearn/utils/tests passes.
Version
1.10.dev0
Interest in fixing/enhancing

title: RFC: Unknown categories should not inherit the meaning of missing values in HGB / trees
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

HistGradientBoosting* and DecisionTree* (native categorical support) both encode a categorical column such that a category never seen during fit is mapped to the exact same internal value as an actual missing value, inheriting whatever meaning missing values happened to have during training. Let's call this policy A.
This is fine when missingness carries no signal. When it does (a common real-world pattern), it's actively harmful: a brand new, unrelated category at prediction time gets confidently assigned the missing-value prediction instead of an uncertain/neutral one.
I experimented with an alternative policy (B): consider missing values as a category of its own (so just a normal category) and encode it as an integer, and encode unknown values as NaNs.
I could not find a real case example where B underperforms A, but I did find an example where B outperforms A
(KDD cup 2009 dataset, churn target, select one single column with informative missing values as X)
I propose to adopt policy B. It's a small behavior change but I don't think it can break or hurt any existing user code.
Note that we made a bigger and ill-documented one on HGB native categorical support and nobody complained... (and this one could have terribly hurt some ML pipelines).
I think the current impact is low because the likelihood of having unknown categories is low for categorical features of at most 255 distinct categories (which is the current limitation for native categorical support). But with #33972, this 255 limitation is removed for extra-trees (which is great) and the impact of policy A vs B becomes more important.
Note: implementing policy B cleanly with an OrdinalEncoder is currently not possible, which is one of the thing that makes me think that we should move forwards on those two issues:

#28892
#34387

title: Zero `sample_weight` raises ValueError in IsolationForest and Bagging estimators when bootstrap=False
body:
Describe the bug
Since 1.8.0, _generate_bagging_indices draws row indices with
random_state.choice(..., replace=bootstrap_samples, p=normalized_sample_weight).
When bootstrap=False, numpy's choice requires at least max_samples non-zero
entries in p, so any sample_weight containing zeros raises
ValueError: Fewer non-zero entries in p than size

Zero-weighting a row is the documented way to exclude it from a fit, and it is what
sample_weight=0 means everywhere else in the library, so this is ordinary input.
IsolationForest is affected on its defaults (bootstrap=False,
max_samples="auto" → min(256, n_samples)). The crash fires whenever
np.count_nonzero(sample_weight) < min(256, n_samples), which for any dataset of
256 rows or fewer means a single zero weight is enough:



n_samples
zero weights needed to crash




80
1


256
1


300
45


1000
745



BaggingClassifier / BaggingRegressor with bootstrap=False are affected the same
way. They at least emit UserWarning: When fitting ... with sample_weight it is recommended to use bootstrap=True; IsolationForest emits nothing before crashing.
This is a regression from #31414 (merged June 2025, first released in 1.8.0). The
behaviour is unchanged on main.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
import numpy as np
from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest

X = np.random.RandomState(0).uniform(size=(80, 4))
w = np.ones(80)
w[0] = 0.0          # exclude exactly one row, the documented way

IsolationForest(random_state=0).fit(X, sample_weight=w)
Expected Results
A fit equivalent to deleting the zero-weighted rows, which is what happens today if
you do the exclusion by hand:
IsolationForest(random_state=0).fit(X[w > 0])   # works fine
Actual Results
Traceback (most recent call last):
  ...
  File ".../sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py", line 143, in _generate_bagging_indices
    sample_indices = random_state.choice(
  File "numpy/random/mtrand.pyx", line 1032, in numpy.random.mtrand.RandomState.choice
ValueError: Fewer non-zero entries in p than size

Suggested fix
Without replacement you can only draw rows that have non-zero weight, so clamp the
request to the available support. Zero-weighted rows are then excluded exactly as if
they had been deleted:
--- a/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py
+++ b/sklearn/ensemble/_bagging.py
@@ -85,6 +85,10 @@ def _generate_bagging_indices(
         )
     else:
         normalized_sample_weight = sample_weight / np.sum(sample_weight)
+        if not bootstrap_samples:
+            # Sampling without replacement can only draw rows that have a
+            # non-zero weight, so requesting more than that is not satisfiable.
+            max_samples = min(max_samples, np.count_nonzero(sample_weight))
         sample_indices = random_state.choice(
             n_samples,
             max_samples,
Verified with this patch applied:

the reproducer above and the Bagging* equivalents all fit;
sklearn/ensemble/tests/test_bagging.py and test_iforest.py pass (160 passed);
over 300 draws, zero-weighted rows are never selected, each draw yields exactly the
70 available non-zero rows, and indices stay distinct;
the bootstrap=True path is untouched and still samples proportionally to weight.

Versions
System:
    python: 3.12.3
   machine: Linux 7.0.0-28-generic

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.8.0        (also reproduced by inspection on main @ 1752fca7b)
        numpy: 2.4.3
        scipy: 1.17.1

title: Document tie-breaking behavior for max_categories in OneHotEncoder/OrdinalEncoder infrequent category grouping
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the issue linked to the documentation
When max_categories forces additional categories into the infrequent group beyond what min_frequency alone would select, and multiple categories are tied in count at the cutoff boundary, the docs for max_categories don't specify which tied category is kept as frequent vs. grouped as infrequent.
Looking at _identify_infrequent() in sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py, the tie-break is implicit rather than documented:
# stable sort to preserve original count order
smallest_levels = np.argsort(category_count, kind="mergesort")[:-frequent_category_count]
infrequent_mask[smallest_levels] = True
Counts are sorted using np.argsort(category_count, kind="mergesort") — a stable sort — so ties are resolved by the order categories appear in categories_[i], which for categories='auto' is lexicographic/numeric sort order. This behavior is not mentioned in the max_categories docstring or the User Guide section on infrequent categories (encoder_infrequent_categories).
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
Add a sentence to the max_categories parameter docs (in both OneHotEncoder and OrdinalEncoder) and to the User Guide section on infrequent categories, stating that ties in category count are broken using the sort order of the categories (via a stable sort). This is also relevant to the discussion in #32161.
Minimal reproducer
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

X = np.array([["a"] * 2 + ["b"] * 2 + ["c"] * 5], dtype=object).T
enc = OneHotEncoder(max_categories=2, sparse_output=False).fit(X)
print(enc.infrequent_categories_)
# 'a' and 'b' tie at count=2 -- which one is grouped as infrequent
# is not documented, though it is deterministic.
Additional context
Related: #32161 discusses tie-breaking by lexicographical order for encoder category ordering more broadly.

title: RandomForest errors out with infinite values for predictions
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
Decision trees have decision rules of the form x <= value and similar. Such rules are well defined for infinite values, and it should be possible to make predictions on them, but scikit-learn refuses such inputs.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
import numpy as np

title: dump_svmlight_file segfaults with multilabel=True and a 1D target array
body:
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
sklearn.datasets.dump_svmlight_file terminates the Python interpreter with a segmentation fault when multilabel=True is combined with a one-dimensional target array.
The input passes the public API parameter validation because y is array-like and multilabel is a boolean. However, the implementation subsequently appears to treat each scalar y[i] as an iterable collection of labels.
The following closely related input combinations work correctly:

A sequence of label sequences such as [[0], [1]] with multilabel=True.
A one-dimensional target array with multilabel=False.

A one-dimensional y may be invalid when multilabel=True, but a public scikit-learn API should reject it with a clear TypeError or ValueError. It should never terminate the entire Python process.
This can crash notebooks, data-processing pipelines, services, or other applications that pass incorrectly structured target data to this function.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
The following self-contained script runs the problematic public API call in a child process because the call terminates the interpreter:
import subprocess
import sys
import tempfile

if len(sys.argv) > 1:
    import numpy as np
    from sklearn.datasets import dump_svmlight_file

    X = np.zeros((2, 2))
    y = np.array([0, 1])

    with tempfile.NamedTemporaryFile(suffix=".svm") as tmp:
        dump_svmlight_file(X, y, tmp.name, multilabel=True)

    raise SystemExit(0)

import sklearn

print("sklearn", sklearn.__version__)

result = subprocess.run(
    [sys.executable, __file__, "child"],
    capture_output=True,
    text=True,
)

status = (
    f"signal {-result.returncode}"
    if result.returncode < 0
    else f"exit {result.returncode}"
)
print(f"  child -> {status}")

if result.returncode < 0:
    print(
        "BUG REPRODUCES: dump_svmlight_file(multilabel=True, 1-D y) "
        "kills the interpreter instead of raising"
    )
    raise SystemExit(1)

print("OK: call raises or returns instead of crashing")
Run it with:
python sklearn-001.py
Expected Results
The function should reject the incompatible combination of multilabel=True and a one-dimensional target array with a Python exception, such as a TypeError or ValueError.
For example:
ValueError: When multilabel=True, y must be a sequence of label sequences.

The Python interpreter should remain alive.
Actual Results
The child process is terminated by SIGSEGV:
sklearn 1.8.0
  child -> signal 11
BUG REPRODUCES: dump_svmlight_file(multilabel=True, 1-D y) kills the interpreter instead of raising

No Python traceback is produced because the interpreter is terminated by the segmentation fault.

title: adding weights to the calculation for Ledoit Wolf
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the workflow you want to enable
Ledoit Wolf is a method for shrinking the empirical covariace matrix for data, and is already available in this library. The process essentially does three steps:

make the empirical covariance matrix
calculates some parameters (beta / delta) that are then used to calculate the shrinkage coefficient
use the results from steps (1) and (2) to make the desired output.

Given random p-vector X,  step (1) is just doing E[ X X^T ) - E[ X ] E[X^T ] the way you expect. Step (2) is calculating variables beta and delta that invariably involve calculating E[ X_i X_j ] and E[ X^2_i X^2_j ], just with a typical mean calculation. What I am proposing is extending these calculations, where weights can be leveraged to do the expected value calculations. This will allow the user to, for example, do the calculation on the exponentially weighted covariance matrix, but really use any weighting they choose. By setting weights = np.ones( X.shape[0] ) by default, we can maintain the current standard output. If desired, this procedure might possibly be extended to OAS (another shrinkage matrix).
Describe your proposed solution
I am proposing adding the named variable "weights" to the "fit" function inputs for the LedoitWolf class (and any other necessary changes under the hood).

title: `UnionFind.fast_find`'s path compression never touches the queried node — quadratic linkage labelling
body:
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
UnionFind.fast_find's path-compression loop never actually shortens the path of the node it was called on, so path compression is effectively disabled. fast_find degenerates to a plain, uncompressed find. Callers that build a dendrogram (e.g. make_single_linkage) allocate a new parent node per merge, so single-linkage/chaining inputs produce O(n)-deep union-find trees; with compression disabled, the repeated uncompressed finds sum to O(n²). This is invisible on small inputs but dominates end-to-end runtime at scale (tens of seconds at n≈200k in a comparable reproduction — see the linked hdbscan report for measured numbers against the same code pattern).
File: sklearn/cluster/_hierarchical_fast.pyx — UnionFind.fast_find
Also affects: sklearn/cluster/_hdbscan/_linkage.pyx::make_single_linkage, which calls UnionFind.fast_find in its inner loop; and, within sklearn/cluster/_agglomerative.py, AgglomerativeClustering(linkage="single") / FeatureAgglomeration(linkage="single"), both of which route through _hierarchical.single_linkage_label / _hierarchical._single_linkage_label (the unconstrained and connectivity-constrained paths, respectively) in linkage_tree(). Other linkages (ward, average, complete) use a separate heap + IntFloatDict implementation and are not affected.
Type: performance (results are correct; time is quadratic)
Related: the same defect exists independently in the hdbscan package (scikit-learn-contrib/hdbscan, hdbscan/_hdbscan_linkage.pyx), which has its own vendored copy of this UnionFind. Bug report: scikit-learn-contrib/hdbscan#731.
LLM usage: found using Claude, reviewed manually.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
import numpy as np, time
from sklearn.cluster._hierarchical_fast import single_linkage_label

def build_L(K):
    rows = []
    w = 0
    for i in range(K - 1):
        rows.append((i, i + 1, w)); w += 1
    for i in range(K):
        rows.append((i, K + i, w)); w += 1
    return np.array(rows, dtype=np.float64)

prev_t = None
for K in [1000, 2000, 4000, 8000, 16000, 32000, 64000]:
    L = build_L(K)
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    single_linkage_label(L)
    t1 = time.perf_counter()
    dt = t1 - t0
    ratio = dt / prev_t if prev_t else None
    print(f'K={K:6d}  n_samples={2*K:6d}  time={dt:.4f}s  ratio={ratio}')
    prev_t = dt
Expected Results
Each doubling increases the runtime by a factor close to 2.
Actual Results

Interest in fixing the bug
The code
# sklearn/cluster/_hierarchical_fast.pyx
cdef class UnionFind(object):

    def __init__(self, N):
        self.parent = np.full(2 * N - 1, -1., dtype=np.intp, order='C')
        self.next_label = N
        self.size = np.hstack((np.ones(N, dtype=np.intp),
                               np.zeros(N - 1, dtype=np.intp)))

    cdef void union(self, intp_t m, intp_t n) noexcept:
        self.parent[m] = self.next_label
        self.parent[n] = self.next_label
        self.size[self.next_label] = self.size[m] + self.size[n]
        self.next_label += 1
        return

    @cython.wraparound(True)
    cdef intp_t fast_find(self, intp_t n) noexcept:
        cdef intp_t p
        p = n
        # find the highest node in the linkage graph so far
        while self.parent[n] != -1:
            n = self.parent[n]
        # provide a shortcut up to the highest node
        while self.parent[p] != n:
            p, self.parent[p] = self.parent[p], n
        return n
Root cause
The "shortcut" line
p, self.parent[p] = self.parent[p], n
is a chained tuple assignment target1, target2 = rhs1, rhs2. Cython (like Python) evaluates the full right-hand side first — as a tuple, using the current value of p — and only then performs the assignments, left to
right:

Evaluate rhs = (self.parent[p], n) using the old p.
Assign target 1: p = rhs[0] — p is rebound now, to its old parent.
Assign target 2: self.parent[p] = rhs[1] — but this indexes with the already-updated p from step 2, not the node the loop meant to compress. The write lands one hop up from where it was intended.

The node originally passed to fast_find(n) is therefore never repointed at the root; only its ancestors shift by one hop per call. Reproducing the assignment in isolation:
>>> parent = [1, 2, 3, -1]          # chain 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3(root)
>>> p, n = 0, 3
>>> p, parent[p] = parent[p], n     # one iteration of the "compression" loop
>>> p, parent
(1, [1, 3, 3, -1])                  # node 0 STILL points at 1 — untouched
Every subsequent fast_find(0) re-walks 0 → 1 → 3, and this compounds across the whole tree, producing the O(n²) behavior.
Impact

Any caller that builds a chained union-find structure and repeatedly calls fast_find on it is quadratic in the number of points, dominated by re-walked, uncompressed paths. This includes make_single_linkage in sklearn/cluster/_hdbscan/_linkage.pyx (used by HDBSCAN) and AgglomerativeClustering(linkage="single") /
FeatureAgglomeration(linkage="single") in sklearn/cluster/_agglomerative.py.
Results are unaffected. fast_find still returns the correct root (the outer while self.parent[n] != -1 loop correctly finds it), so linkage/hierarchy output is unchanged; this is purely a performance bug.

Suggested fix
Walk to the root first, then compress every node on the path in a second pass. This sidesteps the tuple-assignment aliasing trap entirely:
cdef intp_t fast_find(self, intp_t n) noexcept:
    cdef intp_t root, nxt
    root = n
    while self.parent[root] != -1:
        root = self.parent[root]
    while self.parent[n] != -1 and self.parent[n] != root:
        nxt = self.parent[n]
        self.parent[n] = root
        n = nxt
    return root
Roots are unchanged, so output is bit-identical; only the amortized complexity of repeated fast_find calls improves (from effectively uncompressed to near-inverse-Ackermann with compression restored).
Notes

See the companion hdbscan package report (linked at the top of this file) for a worked measurement of the same pattern in a near-identical (ndarray-backed, rather than memoryview-backed) UnionFind.

title: explained_variance_score returns a perfect 1.0 for a single sample (silently breaks LeaveOneOut CV)
body:
Describe the bug
explained_variance_score returns 1.0 (a perfect score) for a single sample no
matter how wrong the prediction is, and emits no warning. r2_score, its
documented sibling, guards the same degenerate case with an
UndefinedMetricWarning and returns nan.
With one sample there is no variance to explain, so the numerator
(Var(y_true - y_pred)) and the denominator (Var(y_true)) are both 0, and
force_finite maps 0/0 to 1.0 — documented as "perfect predictions" — even
when the prediction is plainly wrong.
The practical consequence is that LeaveOneOut cross-validation scored with
explained_variance silently reports a perfect 1.0 for any model, including one
fit on pure noise.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
from sklearn.metrics import explained_variance_score, r2_score
from sklearn.model_selection import LeaveOneOut, cross_val_score

# 1) single sample, clearly wrong prediction
print(explained_variance_score([1.0], [2.0]))  # 1.0, no warning
print(r2_score([1.0], [2.0]))                  # nan + UndefinedMetricWarning

# 2) the practical impact: LeaveOneOut on pure noise
rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
X, y = rng.normal(size=(12, 3)), rng.normal(size=12)

ev = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=LeaveOneOut(),
                     scoring="explained_variance")
r2 = cross_val_score(LinearRegression(), X, y, cv=LeaveOneOut(), scoring="r2")
print(ev.mean())  # 1.0   <- perfect score on noise, silently
print(r2.mean())  # nan   <- correctly undefined
Expected Results
Something that does not claim a perfect fit on a single sample. Matching
r2_score seems most consistent: emit UndefinedMetricWarning and return nan
when n_samples < 2, since the metric is not defined without variance to
explain.
Actual Results
1.0        # explained_variance_score([1.0], [2.0]) -- no warning
nan        # r2_score([1.0], [2.0]) -- UndefinedMetricWarning

1.0        # LeaveOneOut + explained_variance on pure noise
nan        # LeaveOneOut + r2 on pure noise (12 UndefinedMetricWarnings)

Versions
System:
    python: 3.14
Python dependencies:
    sklearn: 1.9.0

Notes
I appreciate that ignoring a systematic offset is intentional for this metric
(the docstring notes it), so the n_samples >= 2 behaviour is not in question
here — only the single-sample case, where there is no variance at all and the
score is silently reported as perfect.
I'm happy to open a PR adding the same n_samples < 2 guard that r2_score
already uses, if that's the direction you'd prefer.

title: Perf: `PCA(n_components="mle")` uses O(d^3) version of Minka's algorithm when O(d^2) exists
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the workflow you want to enable
PCA(n_components="mle") is very slow on large datasets since it runs in O(d^3) where d=min(n_features, n_samples) and has considerable Python loop overhead.
T Minka has an O(d^2) matlab implementation that incidentally would enable much better vectorization:
https://github.com/tminka/tminka.github.io/blob/master/papers/pca/laplace_pca.zip (see laplace_pca.m in that zip)
Describe your proposed solution
We should port that to Python, or at least the core pa reformulation that makes each rank evaluation linear time instead of quadratic. There are a few more tweaks in there, some of which were added years later, that are probably good ideas but would change the behavior of the function slightly. I propose we just port the runtime improvement without changing behavior; future work can look into adapting some of the other improvements.
Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant
No response
Additional context
I'll put together a PR for this.

title: Speed up SelectKBest with partition-based selection
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the workflow you want to enable
basically the title.
the partition based algorithm performs better on the larger(300+) features, so my idea is to keep the already existing algorithm for lower features, while for bigger ones use the partition-based one.
partition based algorithmworks by using np.partition to find the k-th highest score without fully sorting every score, giving average O(n) time instead of O(nlogn).
Scores above that threshold are selected without addutiinal operations
If several scores equal the threshold, the algorithm selects the highest-indexed tied features to match the old stable-sort result.
check for more info:
https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/generated/numpy.partition.html
https://webpages.charlotte.edu/rbunescu/courses/ou/cs4040/introsort.pdf

I would like to propose a new gallery example focused on evaluating Precision-Recall curves on highly imbalanced financial datasets (e.g., payment fraud detection).

In production settings like FinTech, target classes are highly imbalanced (~1-2% positive class), making PR-AUC and threshold tuning critical compared to standard ROC-AUC metrics.

Compare ROC vs. Precision-Recall curves on imbalanced distributions.
Demonstrate threshold selection strategies for high-precision vs. high-recall trade-offs in fraud context.

Dataset generation / loading simulating payment fraud class ratios (make_classification or synthetic imbalance).
Fitting baseline models (e.g., Logistic Regression / Tree-based).

title: RFC Always store fitted attributes as Numpy
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

This is an issue related to #34152 but is also a standalone issue.
While thinking about #34152 and working on #34324 I thought that it might be a good idea if the fitted attributes of an estimator were always Numpy arrays. The current plan is to store fitted attributes in the namespace/device of X.
Reasons to do this:

users most often use fitted attributes for inspection/debugging/plotting. Having them in a consistent array namespace makes this easy to do. If the namespace is input dependent then you have to change your debugging/plotting code. Say you run the same script on a machine with a CUDA GPU and on your laptop with no GPU. While it is not difficult to use write code that uses move_to() to conditionally bring the attributes to Numpy for plotting, it is tedious.
Today attributes are Numpy, by keeping them Numpy we remove one source of bugs/differences. Enabling array API by default would not change this
Part of #34324 that is not great/tricky is dealing with estimators that sometimes support array API. For example for some hyper-parameter values array API is supported and for some not. The tricky question: What should the type of the fitted attributes be?
You can fit with one array namespace/device and predict with a different one without any conversion
An estimator fitted with pytorch/CUDA can be unpickled on a machine without CUDA and even without pytorch

Something to check is how much overhead/performance loss we get in predict and other inference methods if we have to convert the fitted attributes relevant for predicting from Numpy to the array namespace of the input each time. Though I suspect that conversion is fast. It might add appreciable overhead if you are predicting on very few samples, but the absolute time will be short in those cases (and you could just use the CPU?). We would need to introduce a way to make it easy to convert fitted attributes to Numpy in each estimator to avoid lots of boilerplate. What are other reasons to not do this?
What do others think?

title: Explicit documentation / contract for free-threading
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the issue linked to the documentation
Scikit-learn offers builds for free-threaded Python, but it is not clear as a user what is supposed to be safe to call from multiple threads.
For example, it feels quite obvious that one should not call .fit() on the same object from multiple threads even if not documented, but does the interface guarantee that other methods are safe to call on the same object from multiple threads? For instance, KNN depending on the arguments might do most of the work in other methods, and I'm not sure if it doesn't modify any internal attributes starting with underscores.
Further, since lots of other Python libraries offer scikit-learn-compatible objects, it would be quite useful to have official documentation from scikit-learn about what needs or doesn't need to be thread-safe in order to develop scikit-learn-compatible classes.
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
Add a documentation page for free threading covering all these kinds of details, plus additional documentation on a per-estimator basis if needed for exceptions. Mention these thread safety requirements also in the developer guide.

title: Allow TunedThresholdClassifierCV to assess threshold variability and examine all possible thresholds

WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the workflow you want to enable
If I understand this correctly TunedThresholdClassifierCV calculates the metric values at the indicated threshold fo each folds, then takes the average metric per threshold, and with that it selects the best threshold. Would it be possible to also determine the std of the threshold? Mostly for analysis. Would be nice to see how this value compares with Elkan's threshold.
The other request: at the moment, threshold takes an array of cut-off points, 100 by default. To examine all possible cut-offs, particularly important with highly imbalanced data, would it be possible to allow "auto" for example, in which case the cut-off values to examine would be unique(probs), like it's done for roc curves?
Describe your proposed solution
not sure this is the best solution but here it goes:
_mean_interpolated_score already builds a full array of per-fold interpolated curves before reducing it with np.mean(..., axis=0).
The ask would be to also keep np.std(..., axis=0) and expose it (e.g. cv_results_["scores_std and maybe best_score_std_ at the chosen threshold) when store_cv_results=True.

title: RFC Should we require contributors to communicate in their own words (as opposed to posting AI output)?
body:
Here I propose to require contributors to write comments, PR descriptions and issues using their own words, as opposed to posting AI generated text.
Specifically, I really like the Astral AI policy, that explicitly states:

AI should not be used to generate comments when communicating with maintainers. We expect comments on our projects to be written by humans. We may hide any comments that we believe are AI generated.
...
If you are opening an issue, we expect you to describe the problem in your own words.
...
If you wish to include context from an interaction with AI in your comments, it must be in a quote block (e.g., using >) and disclosed as such. It must be accompanied by human commentary explaining the relevance and implications of the context. Do not share long snippets.

Using AI to post long generated summaries on issues and PR descriptions and to comment on how to resolve a certain problem is very impolite / disrespectful anyway. It puts the burden on filtering out the useful information (if any) on the reader. The poster may not be the author and may not understand what they were posting.
If we require contributors to use their own words in written communication we can easier handle the extreme cases by either requests to use their own words or by closing if genuine communication is not possible.

title: asv benchmarks are broken with latest asv_runner
body:
asv_runner has a fun hack now:
    @staticmethod
    def _is_parameter_free_setup(setup):
        """
        True if ``setup`` can be called with no positional arguments.
        Used so module-level ``setup(*args, **kwargs)`` runs before
        ``setup_cache`` while class ``setup(self, n)`` waits for ``do_setup``.
        """
        try:
            inspect.signature(setup).bind()
        except TypeError:
            return False
        return True
Unfortunately this detects the setup() function in asv_benchmarks/benchmarks/common.py as not needing parameters, which breaks benchmarks. The symptom is benchmarks failing to run with error about setup_cache failed.
A hacky workaround:
diff --git a/asv_benchmarks/benchmarks/common.py b/asv_benchmarks/benchmarks/common.py
index c12da551010..eff964a955e 100644
--- a/asv_benchmarks/benchmarks/common.py
+++ b/asv_benchmarks/benchmarks/common.py
@@ -159,8 +159,12 @@ class Estimator(ABC):
             with est_path.open(mode="wb") as f:
                 pickle.dump(estimator, f)
 
-    def setup(self, *params):
+    def setup(self, param1, *params):
         """Generate dataset and load the fitted estimator"""
+        # Stupid hack to workaround fact asv_runner uses ability to call
+        # without any params as semantically significant:
+        params = (param1,) + params
+
         # This is run once per combination of parameters and per repeat so we
         # need to avoid doing expensive operations there.
Perhaps this should be fixed upstream, but recording this here in case someone else needs to run benchmarks.

title: OneHotEncoder: inverse_transform decodes unknown categories as the dropped category (not None) when drop + handle_unknown='ignore'
body:
Describe the bug
When OneHotEncoder is configured with both drop='first' (or any drop) and
handle_unknown='ignore', unknown categories are silently decoded as the
dropped category by inverse_transform, instead of None.
This directly contradicts the documented behavior of handle_unknown='ignore'.
The parameter docstring states:

'ignore' : When an unknown category is encountered during transform, the
resulting one-hot encoded columns for this feature will be all zeros. In the
inverse transform, an unknown category will be denoted as None.

The root cause is an unavoidable encoding collision: the dropped category and an
unknown category are both encoded as the all-zeros vector, so they are
indistinguishable at inverse_transform time. The current implementation
resolves the ambiguity in favor of the dropped category
(sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py, inverse_transform), which means a
round-trip silently rewrites unknown values into a valid, known category with no
warning.
Note there is also an internal documentation inconsistency: the handle_unknown
parameter docstring promises None, while the inverse_transform method
docstring says the dropped category is used. The two contradict each other.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder

ohe = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", drop="first", sparse_output=False)
ohe.fit(np.array([["a"], ["b"], ["c"]]))

X = np.array([["a"], ["b"], ["c"], ["z"]])   # "z" is unknown
encoded = ohe.transform(X)
back = ohe.inverse_transform(encoded)

print("dropped category 'a' ->", ohe.transform([["a"]]))   # [[0. 0.]]
print("unknown   'z'      ->", ohe.transform([["z"]]))      # [[0. 0.]]  (identical!)
print("round-trip:", back.ravel().tolist())
Expected Results
Per the handle_unknown='ignore' documentation, the unknown value should be
decoded as None:
['a', 'b', 'c', None]

Actual Results
The unknown value is silently decoded as the dropped category 'a':
['a', 'b', 'c', 'a']

The dropped category and the unknown category produce the identical all-zeros
encoding [[0. 0.]], so they cannot be told apart on inverse transform, and the
unknown is silently turned into a real category.
Impact
inverse_transform(transform(X)) is not a safe round trip when drop and
handle_unknown='ignore' are combined: unknown/invalid inputs are silently
converted into a valid known category, with no warning. This is an easy
data-integrity footgun in preprocessing pipelines.
Possible resolutions
Some options for discussion:

Fix the handle_unknown docstring to explicitly document that when drop is
set, unknown categories are decoded as the dropped category (documentation
only), and reconcile it with the inverse_transform docstring.
Emit a warning from inverse_transform when the ambiguous drop +
handle_unknown='ignore' combination causes all-zero rows to be decoded as
the dropped category.
Consider disallowing / warning on the ambiguous drop +
handle_unknown='ignore' combination at fit time.

Happy to open a PR once maintainers indicate the preferred direction.
Versions
System:
    Windows-10-10.0.26200-SP0
    Python 3.11.9
Python dependencies:
    scikit-learn: 1.9.0
    numpy:        2.4.6
    scipy:        1.17.1

Behavior also confirmed by source inspection on main
(sklearn/preprocessing/_encoders.py, handle_unknown docstring vs.
inverse_transform).

title: PowerTransformer raises raw TypeError on Pandas nullable integer (Int64) and float (Float64) dtypes containing pd.NA
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
When passing a Pandas DataFrame containing modern nullable extension dtypes (such as Int64 or Float64) with missing values (pd.NA) into PowerTransformer, the estimator crashes with an unhandled internal exception (TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous) rather than coercing the array cleanly or raising a standard scikit-learn ValueError.
Context & User-Facing Impact

Modern Pandas Integration: With modern Pandas workflows (including Pandas 2.0+ defaults and df.convert_dtypes()), nullable integer and float types are standard when working with tabular data that contains missing values.
Pipeline Failures: In production data pipelines, passing a DataFrame with nullable dtypes directly into a scikit-learn Pipeline([('power_transform', PowerTransformer()), ...]) causes the entire pipeline to fail with a low-level Pandas boolean evaluation error instead of processing the data smoothly.
Unnecessary Workarounds: To bypass this bug, users currently have to manually write boilerplate pre-casting logic (e.g., df.astype("float64")) before calling PowerTransformer, which breaks scikit-learn's native DataFrame compatibility goals.
Consistency: Most scikit-learn estimators handle Pandas extension arrays seamlessly by converting them to standard floating-point NumPy arrays via _validate_data. PowerTransformer should follow this same pattern.

Steps/Code to Reproduce
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.preprocessing import PowerTransformer

# Minimal DataFrame using Pandas nullable integer extension dtype ('Int64')
# The missing value (None) is automatically represented as pd.NA
X = pd.DataFrame({"col": pd.Series([1, 2, None, 4], dtype="Int64")})

# Triggers raw TypeError inside PowerTransformer during internal array checks
pt = PowerTransformer(method="box-cox")
pt.fit_transform(X)
Expected Results
PowerTransformer should automatically coerce Pandas nullable extension arrays into standard IEEE floating-point NumPy arrays (np.float64 or np.float32) via _validate_data before evaluating numerical bound checks.
Specifically:

It should not crash with a raw TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous.
Passing data with nullable dtypes should either complete successfully (coercing pd.NA to np.nan) or raise a clear, standardized ValueError if input constraints are violated.

Actual Results
The estimator crashes with a raw TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous during internal positivity checks (X <= 0):
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "reproduce_bug.py", line 9, in <module>
    pt.fit_transform(X)
  File "sklearn/base.py", line 1478, in fit_transform
    return self.fit(X, **fit_params).transform(X)
  File "sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py", line 3218, in fit
    return self._fit(X, y, force_transform=False)
  File "sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py", line 3232, in _fit
    if np.any(X <= 0):
  File "pandas/core/ops/common.py", line 81, in new_method
    return method(self, other)
TypeError: boolean value of NA is ambiguous

### Versions

```shell
System:
    python: 3.12.3
executable: /usr/bin/python3
   machine: Linux-6.8.0-generic-x86_64

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.9.0
        numpy: 2.5.1
        scipy: 1.18.0
       pandas: 3.0.4
   matplotlib: 3.9.0
       joblib: 1.4.2
threadpoolctl: 3.5.0

Interest in fixing the bug
Yes, I am interested in opening a Pull Request to fix this issue once it has been triaged!
Root Cause Analysis
In PowerTransformer._fit (inside sklearn/preprocessing/_data.py), positivity and finite bounds checks—such as np.any(X <= 0)—are executed on the input X before array validation occurs:
# Current order of execution in _fit():
if np.any(X <= 0):  # <--- Fails here on Pandas ExtensionArrays containing pd.NA
    raise ValueError(...)

X = self._validate_data(X, ...)

title: LogisticRegressionCV raises TypeError: make_scorer() got multiple values for keyword argument 'pos_label' with string scoring on binary classification (v1.9 regression)
body:
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
LogisticRegressionCV with scoring="f1_macro" raises a TypeError on binary classification problems in sklearn 1.9. The error does not occur in sklearn 1.8.x.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegressionCV
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
  
X, y = make_classification(n_samples=100, n_features=20, n_classes=2,
  random_state=0)
  
clf = LogisticRegressionCV(cv=3, random_state=0, scoring="f1_macro")
clf.fit(X, y)
Expected Results
The model fits successfully, as it did in sklearn 1.8.x.
Actual Results
Traceback (most recent call last):
    File "<string>", line 8, in <module>
  LogisticRegressionCV(cv=3, random_state=0, scoring='f1_macro').fit(X, y)
    File "sklearn/base.py", line 1403, in wrapper
      return fit_method(estimator, *args, **kwargs)
    File "sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py", line 2279, in fit
  fold_coefs_ = Parallel(n_jobs=self.n_jobs, verbose=self.verbose,
  prefer=prefer)(
          path_func(
          ...
          for l1_ratio in l1_ratios_
      )
    File "sklearn/utils/parallel.py", line 91, in __call__
      return super().__call__(iterable_with_config_and_warning_filters)
    File "joblib/parallel.py", line 1986, in __call__
      return output if self.return_generator else list(output)
    File "joblib/parallel.py", line 1914, in _get_sequential_output
      res = func(*args, **kwargs)
    File "sklearn/utils/parallel.py", line 184, in __call__
      return self.function(*args, **kwargs)
  File "sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py", line 948, in
  _log_reg_scoring_path
      scoring = make_scorer(
          scoring._score_func,
          ...
          **getattr(scoring, "_kwargs", {}),
      )
  TypeError: sklearn.metrics._scorer.make_scorer() got multiple values for
  keyword argument 'pos_label'


Versions
System:
      python: 3.13.13
     machine: macOS-arm64
  
  Python dependencies:
        sklearn: 1.9.0
          numpy: 2.5.1
          scipy: 1.18.0
         joblib: 1.5.3
  threadpoolctl: 3.6.0
       narwhals: 2.24.0
  
  Built with OpenMP: True
Interest in fixing the bug
The issue appears to be introduced by PR #30859 (metadata routing for scorers). When scoring="f1_macro" is passed as a string, it's resolved to a scorer object that now includes pos_label in its metadata/parameters (due to the new metadata routing). Then in _log_reg_scoring_path, the code checks if is_binary and "pos_label" in sig and tries to pass pos_label again via make_scorer(...), resulting in the duplicate keyword argument error.
The f1_macro scorer shouldn't need pos_label (it's a macro average across all classes), but the metadata routing changes appear to have added it to the scorer's signature, triggering the binary-classification code path that re-injects it.

title: Inconsistent `_check_initialized` method: only present on gradient boosting estimators
body:
While reviewing #34495, I noticed that _check_initialized only exists on the gradient boosting estimators and nowhere else in the codebase. The method does nothing but wrap check_is_fitted(self).
Steps to reproduce
from sklearn.ensemble import (
    AdaBoostClassifier,
    GradientBoostingClassifier,
    GradientBoostingRegressor,
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier,
    RandomForestClassifier,
)
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

estimators = [
    GradientBoostingClassifier(),
    GradientBoostingRegressor(),
    HistGradientBoostingClassifier(),
    AdaBoostClassifier(),
    RandomForestClassifier(),
    LogisticRegression(),
]

for est in estimators:
    print(f"{type(est).__name__:32s} _check_initialized? {hasattr(est, '_check_initialized')}")

Results
GradientBoostingClassifier       _check_initialized? True
GradientBoostingRegressor        _check_initialized? True
HistGradientBoostingClassifier   _check_initialized? False
AdaBoostClassifier               _check_initialized? False
RandomForestClassifier           _check_initialized? False
LogisticRegression               _check_initialized? False

Background
I tried to trace how the method was introduced. As far as I can tell it first appeared in 2015 and was never explicitly discussed — the surrounding conversations are all about the apply method. Please correct me if I've missed something:

2015: #5228
2016: #7464
2019: #14545

Questions

Should _check_initialized be generalized across the other estimators — e.g. moved up into BaseEnsemble?
Or should it be removed, since it's a redundant wrapper around check_is_fitted and inconsistent with the rest of the codebase?

title: Consider switching to pyrefly for typechecking
body:
I'd like to propose adding Pyrefly for typechecking - it could either be added alongside mypy as a non-blocking CI check or migrated entirely. Happy to open the PR, checking here first to see if there's interest?
For transparency I work on the Pyrefly team, I've been looking into the performance of mypy vs Pyrefly on real repos and when I tried out sklearn the results looked promising enough that I thought I'd share :)
I did some initial investigation, running locally mypy 2.3.0 vs Pyrefly 1.1.1 (checking sklearn/) which shows Pyrefly is ~29x faster:



Checker
Run




mypy
18.4 s


Pyrefly
0.6 s



How to make the switch:

Add the dependency to the test/lint requirements: pyrefly>=1.1.1.
Add [tool.pyrefly] config mirroring the existing [tool.mypy] config.
[tool.pyrefly]
project-includes = ["sklearn"]                        # matches `mypy sklearn/` in build_tools/linting.sh
search-path = ["."]
project-excludes = ["**/sklearn/externals*"]          # mirrors mypy's exclude
preset = "legacy"                                      # matches mypy's non-strict defaults
ignore-missing-imports = ["joblib.*", "sklearn.externals.*", "*"]  # mirrors ignore_missing_imports + follow_imports=skip

resolve/suppress error code differences There are some differences between the errors pyrefly catches and what mypy does (79 new errors from what I can see running locally, details below), so we could either ignore them  (# pyrefly: ignore [code]) for now or see if there are genuine issues to address. If we opt for removing mypy we could also remove ~80 out of 82 mypy ignores that pyrefly doesn't complain about, so the total ignores would stay roughly the same.

title: Pandas output path fails to reject infinite values during transform
body:
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
When using set_output(transform="pandas"), SelectKBest.transform does not reject infinite values in a pandas DataFrame. This is a regression introduced by PR #25102.
The pandas-output path passes cast_to_ndarray=False to _validate_data, which causes check_array to skip its force_all_finite validation. This allows invalid numeric inputs through transform instead of raising the expected validation error.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif

X_train = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "a": [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0],
        "b": [1.0, 2.0, 1.0, 2.0],
    }
)
y = [0, 0, 1, 1]

selector = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=1).set_output(transform="pandas")
selector.fit(X_train, y)

X_bad = X_train.copy()
X_bad.loc[0, "a"] = np.inf

print("Input containing infinity:")
print(X_bad)
print()

try:
    result = selector.transform(X_bad)
    print("Transform succeeded (no error raised):")
    print(result)
except Exception as exc:
    print("Error:", exc)
Expected Results
The input containing infinity should be rejected during transform:
Input containing infinity:
     a    b
0  inf  1.0
1  1.0  2.0
2  0.0  1.0
3  1.0  2.0

Error: Input X contains infinity or a value too large for dtype('float64').

(This is the behavior when set_output is not used.)
Actual Results
No validation error is raised; transform silently succeeds:
Input containing infinity:
     a    b
0  inf  1.0
1  1.0  2.0
2  0.0  1.0
3  1.0  2.0

Transform succeeded (no error raised):
     b
0  1.0
1  2.0
2  1.0
3  2.0

Versions
scikit-learn 1.9.0
Python 3.11.13
Linux
NumPy 2.4.6
SciPy 1.17.1

Interest in fixing the bug
The pandas-output path should preserve DataFrame containers without changing the estimator's validation behavior. Infinite values should continue to be rejected consistently during transform regardless of the output format setting.

title: GradientBoostingClassifier/Regressor._resize_state raises TypeError instead of ValueError on smaller n_estimators
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
Found this while poking around _gb.py. _resize_state has a check meant to give a clear error if you try to shrink n_estimators:
if total_n_estimators < self.estimators_.shape[0]:
    raise ValueError(
        "resize with smaller n_estimators %d < %d"
        % (total_n_estimators, self.estimators_[0])
    )
self.estimators_[0] is wrong there, it grabs an actual fitted estimator object instead of self.estimators_.shape[0] (the count). Since %d can't print a non-number like that, it crashes with a confusing TypeError instead of giving the intended clean error.
You'd never actually see this through normal fit() calls though, since fit() already checks the same thing earlier and raises its own ValueError first, so _resize_state's version never gets a chance to run. That's also why the existing test for this still passes, it's checking the earlier error, not this one, so the bug's been sitting here unnoticed.
Already got a draft PR ready with the fix and a test, figured I'd open this too just to have it tracked.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
import numpy as np

gb = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators=5)
gb.estimators_ = np.empty((10, 1), dtype=object)
gb._resize_state()
Expected Results
Should raise a clean ValueError, something like: ValueError: resize with smaller n_estimators 5 < 10 instead of crashing with an unrelated TypeError.
Actual Results
TypeError: %d format: a real number is required, not numpy.ndarray
Versions

title: RFC Licencing issues when contributors had sold their copyright to paid platforms
body:
I have come across paid / bounty platforms that pay freelancers to open issues/PRs on OSS projects to test certain prompts and serve for finetuning AI tools. These PRs then get reviewed by maintainers and the resulting code as well as traces created during the process are used as training data for LLMs. Most certainly this data gets forward-sold to the companies developing the most popular AI models. This business model seems to be pretty popular these days.
The problem here is that with code submitted via a paid platform, contributors usually don't hold copyright anymore. They have sold it to the company that paid them. As a result, they are formally not allowed to grant their code to be used with a BSD licence.
What can we do about this?
I've opened PR #34490 to educate contributors. Apart from this:

Can probabl pay for a lawyer who advises us on how to re-write scikit-learn's terms?
We should also make sure probabl as an employer of the labs team grants employees to publish their work under scikit-learn's BSD licence.

The trouble a clean contributing policy could prevent is that years later, when maybe the copyright to PRs on scikit-learn gets sold and executed, we won't need to peel away code that was added by contributors that had actually never owned copyright of their work.
CC @GaelVaroquaux @glemaitre

title: PCA does not follow same namespace checking logic as others
body:
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
In most array API estimator methods that happen after .fit(), if an incompatible input is passed to the method, it throws an informative error message, usually coming from check_same_namespace - for example:
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(100,10))
y = rng.standard_normal(size=X.shape[0])

import dpnp
Xd = dpnp.array(X, device="gpu")

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
Ridge(solver="svd").fit(Xd, y).predict(X)
ValueError: Inputs passed to Ridge.predict() must use the same namespace and the same device as those passed to fit(). Array namespaces used during fit (dpnp) and predict (sklearn.externals.array_api_compat.numpy) differ. You can move the estimator to the same namespace and device as X with: 'from sklearn.utils._array_api import move_estimator_to; xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(X); estimator = move_estimator_to(estimator, xp, device)'

The error type in this case is ValueError.
But PCA's methods like inverse_transform do not use that utility function, erroring out with a less informative message instead, and with the error type being TypeError:

  
    
      scikit-learn/sklearn/decomposition/_base.py
    
    
         Line 193
      in
      bb9df11
    
  
  
    

        
          
           xp, _ = get_namespace(X, self.components_, self.explained_variance_) 
        
    
  


Steps/Code to Reproduce
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.standard_normal(size=(100,10))

import dpnp
Xd = dpnp.array(X, device="gpu")

from sklearn import set_config
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)

from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
PCA().fit(Xd).inverse_transform(X)
Expected Results
ValueError with a similar message as the one thrown by Ridge.
Actual Results
TypeError: Multiple namespaces for array inputs

Versions
Not relevant.

title: Infinite Recursion when using a mock as param for a Mock Classifier
body:
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
For verifying the behaviour of our code, we create a mock classifier that is passed down to the functions to train and optimize our model. In scikit-learn 1.9.0, this creates an infinite recursion, and in case of a heavier mock classifier a memory leak.
The code to reproduce the issue is below. A larger example can be found in this gist: https://gist.github.com/phyk/666b7ef4cabf0becff18bea9d13e9389
For both snippets, you need to run them using pytest to get the behavior.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
from unittest.mock import MagicMock

from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin, clone


class FastMockClassifier(BaseEstimator, ClassifierMixin):
    def __init__(self, learning_rate: float = 0.1) -> None:
        self.learning_rate = learning_rate


def test_clone_recursion_leak() -> None:
    clone(FastMockClassifier(learning_rate=MagicMock()))
Expected Results
Under scikit-learn 1.8, this test just passes.
Actual Results
Under scikit-learn 1.9, this snippet uses an unproportionate amount of memory and time.
Versions
1.9.0
Interest in fixing the bug
Yes, would be available for fixing it.

title: AdaBoostClassifier/Regressor.feature_importances_ has dead error-handling code
body:
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
Found this while poking around _weight_boosting.py. feature_importances_ has this check at the top:
if self.estimators_ is None or len(self.estimators_) == 0:
    raise ValueError("Estimator not fitted, call `fit` before `feature_importances_`.")
estimators_ doesn't exist until you fit the model, so accessing it before fit fails with a plain AttributeError before the code even gets to check "is it None". And after fitting, estimators_ is never empty either.
So that whole ValueError branch is just dead code, nobody's ever going to hit it. Other ensembles like RandomForestClassifier handle this with check_is_fitted(self), which gives a proper NotFittedError instead. Seems worth swapping this to match.
Also noticed while I was in there: there's a separate except AttributeError branch a few lines down for when the base estimator doesn't have feature_importances_ at all (e.g. LogisticRegression). That one's real and reachable, but there's no test for it currently.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
from sklearn.ensemble import AdaBoostClassifier
AdaBoostClassifier().feature_importances_
Expected Results
Should raise a proper NotFittedError (using check_is_fitted(self), like other ensemble methods do), instead of failing with a raw AttributeError.
Actual Results
AttributeError: AdaBoostClassifier object has no attribute estimators_

title: DOC: clarify n_iter_ can be 0 when warm_start=True in LogisticRegression
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the issue linked to the documentation
Describe the issue
When using LogisticRegression with warm_start=True, the n_iter_
attribute reports [0] on subsequent fits if the model has already
converged:
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification

X, y = make_classification(n_samples=100, n_features=4, random_state=0)

clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, warm_start=True, random_state=0)
clf.fit(X, y)
print(clf.n_iter_)  # [7]
clf.fit(X, y)
print(clf.n_iter_)  # [0] — unexpected for users
This is technically correct — lbfgs needs 0 iterations when starting
from an already-optimal point — but it is surprising and undocumented.
Suggested fix
Add a note to the n_iter_ attribute docstring mentioning that
n_iter_ can be 0 when warm_start=True and the model has already
converged from a previous fit.
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
No response

title: [DOC] Improve docstring for `orthogonal_mp`
body:
Describe the issue linked to the documentation
Currently, the rendered documentation for linear_model.orthogonal_mp (source) is missing a formalism and the included LaTeX is not rendered.
Further, looking at the included formalisms, it seems that the notation is changed between this docstring and the User Guide section on Orthogonal Matching Pursuit, which uses a w rather than a gamma.
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
I see two potential fixes:

Updating the docstring formatting and notation. I would suggest standardizing this with what's currently in the User Guide :

    Solves `n_targets` Orthogonal Matching Pursuit problems.
    Each instance of the problem aims to approximate the optimum solution vector, parametrized by the number of non-zero coefficients using
    `n_nonzero_coefs`:

    .. math::
        \underset{w}{\operatorname{arg\,min\,}}  ||y - Xw||^2_2 \text{subject to} ||w||_0 <= n_{nonzero coefs}

    When parametrized by error using the parameter `tol`:

    .. math::
        \underset{w}{\operatorname{arg\,min\,}}  ||w||_0 \text{subject to} ||y - Xw||^2_2 <= tol


Removing this portion of the docstring to direct users towards the formalism in the User Guide, as is done for linear_model.OrthogonalMatchingPursuit.

I'm happy to open a PR with either fix !

title: The PyPI wheel doesn't bundle the right `libgomp` on Linux
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
The PyPI wheel bundles libgomp.so.1.0.0-8.5.0-28.el8_10.alma.1.x86_64.debug which is probably not what we want.
Despite scikit-learn building in manylinux_2_28, whose docs say the toolchain is GCC 14, the bundled OpenMP runtime is effectively AlmaLinux 8 / GCC 8.5-era libgomp.
Codex suggests to add this repair command around here to the linux build:
          CIBW_REPAIR_WHEEL_COMMAND_LINUX: >
            LD_LIBRARY_PATH=/opt/rh/gcc-toolset-14/root/usr/lib64:$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
            auditwheel repair -w {dest_dir} {wheel}
auditwheel repair decides which concrete shared object to copy into scikit_learn.libs (what is bundled in the PyPi wheel). Without help, it resolves the base AlmaLinux 8 runtime. With LD_LIBRARY_PATH pointing to gcc-toolset first, it should resolve to the newer gcc-toolset libgomp.

import threadpoolctl

for info in threadpoolctl.threadpool_info():
