title: KMeans can skip final label reassignment after empty-cluster relocation and return stale labels_/inertia_
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
I think there is a convergence bug in KMeans when empty-cluster relocation happens during an iteration.
In both _kmeans_single_lloyd and _kmeans_single_elkan, the main loop checks for strict convergence with:
if np.array_equal(labels, labels_old):
    strict_convergence = True
    break
This check happens after the centers have been updated/swapped. If strict_convergence is true, the final E-step is skipped. That final E-step is otherwise used to make sure the returned labels_ match the final cluster_centers_.
The problem is that empty-cluster relocation can mutate centers_new and weight_in_clusters without mutating labels. So labels can be unchanged from the previous iteration, while the centers have still changed because an empty cluster was repaired. In that case, the algorithm declares “strict convergence” even though the returned centers and labels are inconsistent.
Relevant code paths:

_kmeans_single_lloyd checks np.array_equal(labels, labels_old) and skips the final E-step on strict convergence:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/cluster/_kmeans.py
_kmeans_single_elkan has the same strict-convergence/final-E-step structure:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/cluster/_kmeans.py
_relocate_empty_clusters_dense / _relocate_empty_clusters_sparse modify centers_new and weight_in_clusters, using labels, but do not update labels:
https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/blob/main/sklearn/cluster/_k_means_common.pyx

Steps/Code to Reproduce
import numpy as np
from scipy import sparse
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans

X = sparse.csr_matrix(np.array([[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]]))
init = np.array([[4.0], [0.0], [1.0]])

for algorithm in ["lloyd", "elkan"]:
    km = KMeans(
        n_clusters=3,
        init=init,
        n_init=1,
        max_iter=10,
        tol=0,
        algorithm=algorithm,
        verbose=1,
    ).fit(X)

    print("\n", algorithm)
    print("centers: ", km.cluster_centers_.ravel())
    print("labels_: ", km.labels_)
    print("predict: ", km.predict(X))
    print("inertia_:", km.inertia_)
    print("score:   ", km.score(X))
Expected Results
After fit, the returned labels_, cluster_centers_, and inertia_ should be mutually consistent.
In particular, these should pass:
np.testing.assert_array_equal(km.labels_, km.predict(X))
np.testing.assert_allclose(km.inertia_, -km.score(X))
This also matches the documented behavior that, after the last iteration, labels_ are reassigned to make them consistent with predict on the training set.
Actual Results
For both lloyd and elkan, I get:
Iteration 0, inertia 2.0
Iteration 1, inertia 0.5
Converged at iteration 1: strict convergence.

centers:  [3. 2. 1.]
labels_:  [2 2 0]
predict:  [2 1 0]
inertia_: 1.0
score:    -0.0

The fit also emits:
ConvergenceWarning: Number of distinct clusters (2) found smaller than n_clusters (3).

However, that warning appears to be based on the stale returned labels_: using the final returned centers, predict(X) assigns the three samples to all three clusters.
The returned labels_ do not match predict(X), even though both are using the returned final centers.
Also, inertia_ is inconsistent with score(X): stored inertia is 1.0, while recomputing from the final centers/assignments gives 0.0.
Versions
System:
    python: 3.12.3 (main, Mar 23 2026, 19:04:32) [GCC 13.3.0]
executable: /home/remim/dev/clustering/.venv/bin/python
   machine: Linux-6.6.114.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2-x86_64-with-glibc2.39

Python dependencies:
      sklearn: 1.8.0
          pip: 26.1.1

        scipy: 1.17.1
       Cython: None

Built with OpenMP: True

        version: 0.3.31.188.0
threading_layer: pthreads
   architecture: Haswell

    num_threads: 12

       filepath: /home/remim/dev/clustering/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/scipy.libs/libscipy_openblas-6cdc3b4a.so

Interest in fixing the bug
A fix would be for the empty-cluster relocation routines to report whether a relocation actually happened, and then only allow strict convergence when no relocation occurred:
if np.array_equal(labels, labels_old) and not relocated_empty_clusters:
    strict_convergence = True
    break
I would be interested in opening a PR myself after the issue has been triaged.

title: Test infrastructure and documentation to identify unexpected mutation in parallel code
body:
Describe the workflow you want to enable
To ensure thread-safety, it's useful to have test infrastructure that will provide:

A way to identify thread-safety issues in code that has previously mostly been run in process pools. Free-threading's lack of GIL makes thread safety issues more likely than in the past.
A way to prevent future changes to the code introducing new thread-safety problems.
🆕 A way to identify which parts of a data structure are intended to be thread-safe, and which are not.

A good starting point here is focusing on operations that are already parallel, where users might reasonably expect to be able to turn threading on as a joblib backend and have it Just Work. These operations also work in a very particular way: create some tasks, run them in a worker pool, get back the results of the tasks.
What can go wrong in this particular idiom? Switching from a process pool to a thread pool introduces thread-safety issues with the inputs to a Parallel() operation: whereas mutating in a process is fine, mutating in a thread can affect other threads, or future interactions with the object in the main thread.
This suggests a starting point for a invariant to be using in testing: the inputs to a Parallel() operation that can correctly run with both process and thread pools should not change when the function is run.
🆕 This invariant will not be true for objects that are designed to be mutated safely, so there needs to be a way to opt out of the check.
Describe your proposed solution
When pytest is run (no extra flags! 🆕) and Parallel()'s backend a thread pool

Arguments passed to functions called in parallel are tracked to see if they changed as part of execution.
"Change" is calculated heuristically, with a hash.
If hashes change, raise an AssertionError.

🆕 There will be a mechanism to opt-out parameters, or parameter's attributes, from the hashing. In particular, they can be optionally be marked as one of:

thread-safe: indicating these attributes are designed to be safely mutated from multiple threads. This should include a short explanation or pointer to explanation.
buggy-thread-unsafe: indicating this is not thread-safe but is still being accessed from multiple threads. This should include a reference to a GitHub issue explaining the problem.

In addition to opt-in out of the hashing test, these will therefore also serve as documentation of thread-safety or lack thereof. They can also suggest utility classes to formalize certain idioms that repeat, e.g. one can imagine a Rust-style lock that wraps an object, rather than having lock and lock-protected-object being two different parameters. Such classes would then also be automatically opted-out.
When pytest is first run with the hashing, it will fail in three ways; initial tests suggest perhaps 20 locations are affected:

Known thread-unsafe code: For example, BinaryTree. This can be annotated with ThreadSync, with pointer to an existing issue.
Thread-safe code: E.g. a result objects that is intended to used with a paired lock, an idiom used in at least one place. In this case, this can be annotated and perhaps an issue filed about formalizing the idiom into a reusable class.
Unknown status: Depending how complex it is to investigate, and the investigation's conclusion, either thread-safe or buggy-thread-unsafe with issue filed to investigate it further and determine the final status.

At the end of this relatively quick process the tests should pass across the board, some new issues should be filed for follow up, and a new passing CI job can be added.
Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant
Thread sanitizers can catch some of these issues, and they should be used to validate scikit-learn thread safety over the long term. However, they are not something a developer can easily run locally: they require recompiling CPython and all relevant extensions (though there is a Docker image, but still). Whereas this approach is just a normal Python build running normal Python tests.
Additional context
Based on #34057, but with more details and addressing some concerns in the discussion there.
#34071 would be needed to have this run broadly.
Differences from PR are marked with 🆕, and include:

Added use case of identifying which parts of data structure are designed to be mutable from multiple threads.
Added notions of marking known-thread-safe code and known-buggy code.
Removed notion of pytest flag, just do the test automatically.
Removed notion of switching thread pools on automatically.

title: Opt-in to using thread pools for all parallelism (or almost all)
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the workflow you want to enable
User perspective: By default, most parallelism in sklearn uses process pools. On free-threaded Python, however, threading may well have lower overhead: certainly less memory, but quite possibly it will be faster as well.

There are exceptions. E.g. as discussed in #34070, parallel algorithms that can only use a limited number of cores may be better run as process pools.

The user experience should ideally be "use a thread pool if it's known to be faster." But it's difficult to be sure in the short term whether that's true without further work. And maybe it's situational.
Until sklearn reaches the point where it's automatically choosing the fastest option, in the short term a user would want to be able try as easily as possible to see if threads everywhere speed things up.
Maintainer perspective: When testing for thread-safety, or benchmarking for speed, it's useful to be able to have all parallel algorithms use thread pools by default, whether in a CI job or in local testing.
Describe your proposed solution
Add an environment variable SKLEARN_DEFAULT_PARALLEL_BACKEND that can be set to the relevant joblib backends (loky/threading/serial).
Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant

An env variable could be added to joblib, and then it would be JOBLIB_DEFAULT_PARALLEL_BACKEND.
This could be a Python API, but that means e.g. pytest needs to grow more options so it can call the API, and puts (a bit) more burden on users who want to experiment.
Free-threaded CPython builds could opt-in to thread pools by default. In the long term this may be a better option, in the short term I'd worry about correctness; seems better to change defaults here incrementally.

Additional context
This breaks out one tiny aspect of #34057, where this was done as part of a flag to pytest, and I received feedback disliking such flags. And also this is more generally useful.

title: Prevent CPU over-subscription when using thread pools, similar to what process pools do
body:
Describe the workflow you want to enable
Process pools in sklearn will limit the number of threads used by OpenMP and BLAS. Thread pools will not set any limits.
Consider the following program, which lists how many threads are set for OpenMP/OpenBLAS/etc:
import joblib, sys
from sklearn.utils.parallel import Parallel, delayed
import threadpoolctl

def print_thread_pool_sizes():
    for info in threadpoolctl.threadpool_info():
        print(info["user_api"], info["internal_api"], f"threads: {info['num_threads']}")

with joblib.parallel_config(backend=sys.argv[1]):
    Parallel(n_jobs=-1)([delayed(print_thread_pool_sizes)()])
When run under the default backend, the loky process pool, I get:
$ python nested-parallelism.py loky
blas openblas threads: 1
blas openblas threads: 1
openmp openmp threads: 1

When run under the threading joblib backend, I get:
$ python nested-parallelism.py threading
blas openblas threads: 20
blas openblas threads: 20
openmp openmp threads: 20

This can lead to significant CPU oversubscription, depending on the semantics of the library:

When using OpenBLAS, you will get a total of 40 (20 + 20) threads, since the limit is for a single thread pool shared by the whole process.
When using OpenMP, you will get 400 (20 * 20) threads, since the limit is per operation starting a thread pool.

The result is code that runs slower, wasting CPU cycles, and not actually achieving any more work.
Describe your proposed solution
There are a number of scenarios:
Scenario 1: All cores: If the number of threads in a thread pool is the same as the number of (available) CPU cores, setting the OpenMP/BLAS limit to 1 will work correctly: no oversubscription, no cores sitting idle.
Scenario 2: All cores but 1 or 2: If the requested number of threads/processes is negative number -N in joblib, this is defined as "number of available cores + 1- N". I.e. this semantically suggests the users wants to saturate the cores, but leave a few cores for other tasks. Typically N will be small, e.g. 2 to leave one core free but use all others. In this case again setting the OpenMP/BLAS limit to 1 is the right thing to do.
Scenario 3: A hard-coded small number of cores, less than available cores: The remaining case is most likely when the number of cores is limited due to the way the algorithm works. For process pools joblib will already automatically set the number of threads in OpenMP/BLAS to max(cpu_count() // effective_n_jobs, 1). So for example if you have 10 cores and only starting a pool of size 5, OpenMP/BLAS will each be set to allow 2 threads. In a process pool, this works fine.
For a top-level thread pool, this heuristic works fine for OpenMP but not OpenBLAS, since the meaning of "2" is different: for OpenMP it means "2 threads for every operation started in the 5 threads, for a total of 2 * 5 == 10 threads", for OpenBLAS it means "2 threads for the whole process, for a total of 5 + 2 threads."
So this suggests two options; one could choose one, the other, or both:

Documentation for algorithms with limited parallelism, suggesting that it's better to use processes in order to utilize all cores.
Custom settings per parallelism mechanism: set OpenMP to max(cpu_count() // effective_n_jobs, 1) and BLAS to cpu_count(). This could still lead to oversaturation in certain edge cases, but perhaps it's not as bad.


As a follow-up it looks like MKL at least can due OpenMP-style configuration, with a different API than the one threadpoolctl uses.

Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant
This could be implemented in joblib, rather than in sklearn, but that's a more generic context; there are additional threaded libraries that it might grow support for over time, whereas sklearn has more restricted set. Still, this arguably also be done as the default joblib policy for thread pools.
Additional context
joblib.cpu_count() is aware of CPU resource constraints when running inside Linux containers, so its notion of "all available cores" is usually quite accurate.
I am happy to implement this.
I have also tested this on actual code, and OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 on an all-cores thread pool makes the resulting calculation run faster and reduce involuntary context switches. This is not a perfect experiment since OpenBLAS in threaded mode is often slower than single-threaded OpenBLAS for small tasks, so a better experiment would be with some code that uses OpenMP, if someone can suggest one.

title: Callbacks x Metadata-routing
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

There are 2 (related) things to figure out to enable callbacks to be compatible with metadata-routing. I think it's the first thing to solve before starting to implement callback support in more estimators.


Do we want to allow passing arbitrary metadata to the callbacks ?
my_business_metric.set_score_request(amount=True)
callback = ScoringMonitor(scoring=my_business_metric)
LogisticRegression().set_callbacks(callback).fit(X, y, amount=amount)
I'm not sure that it's very interesting for the ScoringMonitor. Do we think that anyone is interested in the evolution of a business metric during fit ?
Same question for early stopping. Is it something that people do ?
That being said, even if not useful for these callbacks, that may be useful for custom callbacks that I haven't thought about.
What does that require ?
Basically make every estimator a router. And callbacks as well.
That's not a major difficulty but it means that implementing callback support is tied to metadata-routing if you want full capacity (it might be possible to make it optional and then callbacks would be limited when there's no metadata-routing, as it's the case now)


How to handle X_val ?
Assuming that we do the above point, we're facing a major issue with how X_val is treated right now, that is as regular metadata. Consider the following:
my_business_metric.set_score_request(amount=True)
callback = ScoringMonitor(scoring=my_business_metric, eval_on="val")
LogisticRegression().set_callbacks(callback).fit(X, y, X_val=X_val, y_val=y_val, amount_train=amount, amount_val=amount_val)
LogisticRegression is not a consumer of amount: it has no idea which one is for which set. In fact amount_train is not even useful here so I could have just passed amount=amount_val.
X_val and y_val themselves could arguably be consumed by the estimator (at least there are estimators that transform X so X_val should follow).
Another thing is: if we request amount on the scorer then how do we sort out how amount_train and amount_val are forwarded to the scorer ?
All of it comes to me from the fact that X_val is considered regular metadata while it's not really metadata, it's more a secondary dataset with possibly associated metadata. I'm under the impression that the solution lies in the metadata-routing framework rather than in the callbacks, by differentiating from the start metadata associated the train set and metadata associated to the validation set.

title: Inconsistent type of predictions and `classes_` for array API classifiers
body:
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
There's currently 2 classifiers with array API support:

LogisticRegression
RidgeClassifier

The docs and discussions in this issue tracker are quite unclear about what should be the expected behavior when input types are mixed in the case of classifiers.
Since in general 'y' can be something like strings or non-sequential integers that get re-encoded internally, I think it makes sense that the classes_ attributes under array API would be obtained from the type of 'y' and then sliced when returning something from .predict() - i.e. "prediction follows 'y'".
This appears to be the case for LogisticRegression:
import os
os.environ["SCIPY_ARRAY_API"] = "1"

import numpy as np
import torch

rng = np.random.default_rng(seed=123)
X = rng.random(size=(20,3))
y = rng.integers(2, size=X.shape[0])
yt = torch.tensor(y, device="xpu", dtype=torch.float32)

from sklearn import set_config
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
set_config(array_api_dispatch=True)
model = LogisticRegression(solver="lbfgs").fit(X, yt)
model.classes_
tensor([0., 1.], device='xpu:0')

But the docs state "everything follows 'X'" instead, and RidgeClassifier does appear to follow this logic from the docs, even if it might not be as natural for classification scenarios:
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeClassifier
model = RidgeClassifier(solver="svd").fit(X, yt)
model.classes_
array([0., 1.], dtype=float32)

Steps/Code to Reproduce
Described above.
Expected Results
All classifiers with array API support should work like in LogisticRegression.
Actual Results
RidgeClassifier works differently.

title: Should `move_to` handle non-array API inputs?
body:

Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
Internal utility move_to appears to handle cases like Pandas series correctly with most array API namespaces. For example, it works correctly when extracting the namespace and device from libraries like dpnp and array-api-strict and passing those as arguments to move_to, but it doesn't always work with pytorch.

import pandas as pd

x = torch.arange(10)

xp, _, device = get_namespace_and_device(x)
y = move_to(y, xp=xp, device=device)

title: BUG: Silent float32 upcasting to float64 in Pipeline/StandardScaler causes 2x memory bloat
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
When processing massive financial tick data (e.g., shape (10_000_000, 50)), quant systems typically cast down to np.float32 to keep the data within RAM limits.
However, passing a float32 NumPy array through a Pipeline containing a StandardScaler silently upcasts the transformed output back to float64. This creates a silent memory copy that doubles the RAM requirement, frequently triggering Out-Of-Memory (OOM) kills on high-frequency streaming applications.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

# Generate a mock financial tick dataset in float32
X_financial_ticks = np.random.randn(1_000_000, 10).astype(np.float32)

print(f"Input dtype: {X_financial_ticks.dtype}")
print(f"Input memory: {X_financial_ticks.nbytes / 1e6} MB")

# Pass through a standard pipeline
pipeline = Pipeline([
    ('scaler', StandardScaler())
])

X_transformed = pipeline.fit_transform(X_financial_ticks)

print(f"Output dtype: {X_transformed.dtype}")
print(f"Output memory: {X_transformed.nbytes / 1e6} MB")

title: LinearSVC crammer_singer reports a garbage n_iter_
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

TL;DR LinearSVC(multi_class="crammer_singer") with ≥3 classes returns a
garbage n_iter_ and raises a spurious ConvergenceWarning on nearly every fit
(even at max_iter=10_000_000). The Crammer–Singer solver is a single joint
optimization over all classes, so it inherently has exactly one iteration
count — unlike the one-vs-rest path, which trains nr_class independent binary
solvers and genuinely has one n_iter per class. The bug is that the readout
machinery treats CS as if it were OvR with per-class counts: in
sklearn/svm/src/liblinear/linear.cpp, train() correctly allocates one
int for model_->n_iter in the MCSVM_CS branch, but get_n_iter() copies
nr_class slots — it guards the binary case (nr_class == 2) but not
MCSVM_CS, so slots [1..K-1] are out-of-bounds heap reads (non-deterministic
across processes). _fit_liblinear then warns off max(n_iter_).
One-line fix:
treat MCSVM_CS as a single slot in get_n_iter().
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
For LinearSVC(multi_class="crammer_singer") with three or more classes,
clf.n_iter_ does not report the number of iterations the Crammer–Singer solver
actually ran. It reports a large, run-to-run unstable integer drawn from
out-of-bounds reads of the LIBLINEAR heap. As a downstream consequence,
_fit_liblinear then compares this garbage value against max_iter and emits
ConvergenceWarning on essentially every fit — including fits where the solver
converged in a few thousand epochs and max_iter is set to 10_000_000.
User-facing impact:


clf.n_iter_ is not a usable signal for CS. It changes between Python
processes (ASLR re-rolls the heap layout on each execve), so any code that
inspects it — hyper-parameter search summaries, learning-curve diagnostics,
user-written convergence checks — sees noise.


Because the garbage almost always exceeds max_iter, ConvergenceWarning
fires on every CS fit with K ≥ 3, even when the solver has converged. The
recommended remedy (raising max_iter) doesn't help.


Every a few times even 10_000_000 max_iter raises convergence warning.


Steps/Code to Reproduce
import warnings
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.svm import LinearSVC
from sklearn.exceptions import ConvergenceWarning

X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)   # K=10 classes; any K>=3 triggers the bug

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always", ConvergenceWarning)
    clf = LinearSVC(
        multi_class="crammer_singer",
        max_iter=10_000_000,   # absurdly large — bug still fires
        random_state=0,
        dual=True,
    ).fit(X, y)
    warn_fired = any(
        issubclass(w.category, ConvergenceWarning) for w in caught
    )

print("clf.n_iter_      :", clf.n_iter_)
print("ConvergenceWarn? :", warn_fired)
On my machine it fires 3 out of 10 times which is obviously absurd.
Mechanism — three cooperating defects:


Allocation site (sklearn/svm/src/liblinear/linear.cpp): train()
allocates exactly one int for model_->n_iter in the MCSVM_CS branch
and writes only slot [0]:
model_->n_iter = Malloc(int, 1);
// ...
model_->n_iter[0] = Solver.Solve(model_->w);


Out-of-bounds read : get_n_iter() copies
nr_class slots into the caller's buffer. There is a special case for
nr_class == 2 (the binary path, which also allocates one slot), but no
case for MCSVM_CS:
void get_n_iter(const model *model_, int* n_iter)
{
    int labels = model_->nr_class;
    if (labels == 2)      // binary special-cased correctly...
        labels = 1;
                          // ...but MCSVM_CS with K>=3 still loops K times
    if (model_->n_iter != NULL)
        for (int i = 0; i < labels; i++)
            n_iter[i] = model_->n_iter[i];   // slots [1..K-1] are OOB reads
}


Warning fired off the wrong value (sklearn/svm/_base.py):
n_iter_max = max(n_iter_)   # dominated by heap garbage in slots [1..K-1]
if n_iter_max >= max_iter:
    warnings.warn("Liblinear failed to converge, ...")
LinearSVC._classes.py then stores self.n_iter_ = n_iter_.max().item(),
exposing the same garbage value to the user as a scalar int.


Expected Results
clf.n_iter_ is a small positive integer reflecting the number of CS epochs
actually run (a few thousand on this dataset), and ConvergenceWarning is not
raised because the solver converged well within max_iter.
Actual Results
clf.n_iter_ is a large integer that has no relation to the number of epochs the
solver ran, and changes between Python processes. Example output on Linux x86_64
/ glibc:
clf.n_iter_      : 856261606
ConvergenceWarn? : True

The warning text is the standard one:
ConvergenceWarning: Liblinear failed to converge, increase the number of iterations.

The internal n_iter_ buffer (the numpy array _fit_liblinear returns before
LinearSVC.fit collapses it to a scalar via .max().item()) shows what is
actually happening:
slot 0 (real epoch count) : 8401       ← solver converged; well below max_iter=10_000_000
slots 1..9 (garbage)      : [25114, 0, 0, -244463840, 232920324, 1249, 0, 2, 0]
max(n_iter_)              : 232920324  ← heap contents reinterpreted as int32; this is what becomes clf.n_iter_

title: RFC/META Harden CI security
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Because of the ongoing Mini Shai Hulud attack against CI & OSS supply chain (see Postmortem: TanStack npm supply-chain compromise for details), I think we should review and possibly straighten our CI before releasing 1.9.
In particular, we use the unsafe pull_request_target in several workflows which is a documented attack vector of the Mini Shai-Hulud worm that currently still spreads by corrupting an increasing number of npm and pypi packages.
Short term:

Regularly check that the dates of https://pypi.org/project/scikit-learn/#files match our manually triggered release dates (this seems to be the case as of today 2026-05-13)
Review our publish_pypi.yml and wheels.yml workflows to make sure it is not subject by cache poisoning attacks (from a cursory glance it does not think we use any build cache, but we should double-check).
Review findings reported by zizmor .github/workflows/publish_pypi.yml and zizmor .github/workflows/wheels.yml.
Assess if workflows that use pull_request_target can have a side effect on our release process.

Note: I asked the following to Claude: https://claude.ai/share/c6aea06a-a9dc-4e55-b5f4-830254166994 (TL;DNR it isn't too worried, but we should probably spend more time reading this analysis in more details).


Unzip and review the contents of the generated wheel files in the release branch prior to uploading to look for unexpected payload.

EDIT: I asked Claude (same conversation as the one linked above) to do that on the latest nightly wheel and it did not find anything fishy.



Medium/Long term

Hash-pin all github actions used in the publish_pypi.yml and wheels.yml workflows.
Use relative dependency cooldown for GitHub Actions updates via dependabot:

https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/reference/supply-chain-security/dependabot-options-reference?versionId=free-pro-team%40latest&productId=code-security&restPage=tutorials%2Csecure-your-dependencies%2Cautomating-dependabot-with-github-actions#cooldown-


Find ways to avoid the use of pull_request_target in our regular dev CI.
Address any remaining "findings" reported by running zizmor . in our repo (currently 191 findings (73 suppressed, 32 fixable): 4 informational, 26 low, 1 medium, 87 high, many of which are related to pull_request_target and unpinned action references).
Use relative dependency cooldowns when generating lock files as soon as implemented in mamba and conda-lock:

conda/conda-lock#908
mamba-org/mamba#4228


Isolate the release process in a dedicated repo with a easy to audit, limited number of config files/action logs/user permissions, see:

numpy/numpy#29178
https://github.com/numpy/numpy-release
https://github.com/scipy/scipy-release



I labeled this PR as block as I think we should at least do the short terms items prior to releasing.
We can probably create sub-issues for things we agree are good ideas.

title: Use automatic chunk size in `ledoit_wolf_shrinkage` (and friends?)
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

This issue is a tracker for the task of adding chunking to the computation in ledoit_wolf_shrinkage (sklearn/covariance/_shrunk_covariance.py).
For the CPU implementation chunking is already supported. For the array API path we currently perform no chunking. Bigger chunks are better for GPU devices (in terms of execution time), but they require more memory.
After investigating and benchmarking a bit, I am not sure what we should do. For "tall and skinny" datasets blocking doesn't matter. For wide datasets it limits how much additional memory is used for temporaries. With n_features=20_000 you'd use something like 1.6GB of extra memory without blocking. However, the speedup (MPS over numpy) when using blocking is much smaller than if the MPS implementation runs without blocking. It can be  5x - 10x without blocking and only something like 2x faster if you use block_size=1000 for MPS as well.
Numpy is also faster if you increase the block size. For example, block_size=2000 seems to speed things up by roughly a factor two and still only uses a small amount of memory.
So I think we could increase the block size, even for Numpy. But I am not sure how we should decide the trade-off between speed up and memory. We could use a block size like 3000 for all namespaces/devices to get most of the speed up and avoid catastrophic "out of memory" exceptions. The user could then tune the block size if they knew that they have enough memory? But it feels like I just made up 3000, it could equally be 4000 or 2000 - I couldn't argue which of these is more correct/better.
Quoting @ogrisel's comment here to make it easy to find:

I suspect that for CPU devices (e.g. NumPy), the optimal block size should be set that the sum of intermediate arrays stays in Level 3 CPU cache (typically a few megabytes on most modern CPUs).
It should be possible to tell if a given device is CPU or not using something like getattr(array, "__dlpack_device__", lambda: (1, 0))()[0] in (1, 3).

A suggestion is to switch to using block_size="auto" as the default (instead of 1000). This would allow us to use a different value for different devices (eg CPUs vs GPUs). Maybe we could even determine the "best" size based on the L3 cache size, but maybe this is making things too complicated.
xref https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33573/changes#r3028299959

title: Improve `pairwise_distances` so that it works with array API inputs for all supported metrics
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

The pairwise_distances function can't always be called when using array API. We should fix this.
pairwise_distances with metric="mahalanobis" (and other scipy-delegated metrics not in PAIRWISE_DISTANCE_FUNCTIONS) does not work with array API inputs on non-CPU devices.
The "mahalanobis" metric is not in scikit-learn's PAIRWISE_DISTANCE_FUNCTIONS, so pairwise_distances falls through to the scipy fallback path, which calls scipy.spatial.distance.cdist / scipy.spatial.distance.pdist. As of scipy 1.17.1, both functions call np.asarray() on their inputs, which fails for GPU tensors (e.g. PyTorch MPS/CUDA, CuPy).
I'm not sure if the solution for this is to implement this in scikit-learn or wait for scipy to add support for it. For other metrics we have implementations in Python in sklearn/metrics/pairwise.py, so maybe there is no performance downside to having a Python implementation? If yes, then this is "just" a question of turning the handle to implement new distances?
xref https://github.com/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/pull/33573/changes#r3079594482

After tracking down the problem, my understanding is that the CountVectorizer is failing because all strings in the column are shorter than the minimum value in ngram_range (see the example).

title: [FEA] Add Ambiguity Range metric for safety-critical classification
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the workflow you want to enable
Practitioners in safety-critical fields—such as medical diagnostics, structural engineering, or high-stakes financial modeling—require a method to explicitly quantify the "Indecision Zone" of a binary classifier.
While aggregate metrics like the F1-score or Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) provide a high-level view of model performance, they often mask the specific regions where a model's prediction is statistically equivalent to guessing. By implementing the ambiguity_range_score, we enable a Tri-Modal Decision Workflow:
Automated Action (High Confidence): Samples with scores above the Upper Threshold ($T_{upper}$, representing 100% Precision) or below the Lower Threshold ($T_{lower}$, representing 100% Recall) are handled automatically by the system with high trust.
Human-in-the-Loop (Ambiguity Zone): Samples falling within the range $\mathcal{A} = T_{upper} - T_{lower}$ are flagged for manual expert review.
Reliability Benchmarking: This allows developers to select models that minimize required human intervention by reducing the Ambiguity Range, even in cases where traditional metrics like AUC remain static.
Safety-Critical Calibration: Practitioners can visualize exactly how much of a population falls into a "Gray Zone" where the model cannot guarantee a certain outcome.
Describe your proposed solution
I propose adding a new metric: ambiguity_range_score(y_true, y_score, *, epsilon=0.0, pos_label=None).
Key Technical Implementations:
The Ambiguity Measure ($\mathcal{A}$): Defined as the difference between the threshold required for perfect precision and the threshold required for perfect recall.
Epsilon ($\epsilon$) Robustness: To handle real-world datasets containing outliers or label noise, the epsilon parameter allows for a "Soft Ambiguity" measure (e.g., $\epsilon=0.01$ for 99% precision/recall). This prevents a single mislabeled data point from artificially maximizing the range to 1.0.
Integration: The function utilizes the existing precision_recall_curve logic to find the critical boundary points, ensuring consistency with scikit-learn’s internal API.
Threshold Independence & Model Robustness
A common limitation of standard classification metrics is their dependence on an arbitrary decision threshold (e.g., 0.5). Choosing a single threshold is often a heuristic choice made during deployment that may not reflect the inherent separability of the model.
The ambiguity_range_score is superior in this regard because it is threshold-independent. Rather than evaluating performance at a single point, it quantifies the "Indecision Zone" as a global characteristic of the model's feature-space quality. By measuring the distance between the two extreme bounds of reliability ($T_{upper}$ and $T_{lower}$), it provides a scalar value that describes model "resoluteness" regardless of where an individual user might eventually set their operating point.
Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant
I have considered using the Detection Error Tradeoff (DET) curve; however, while DET curves are excellent for visual analysis, they do not provide a direct, scalar "range" value that can be easily used for automated model selection or as a clear KPI for "Human-in-the-Loop" resource planning.
Additional context
I have attached a figure that provides an empirical verification of the metric:
Distribution Density Plot: Illustrates the score overlapping that generates the Ambiguity Range ($\mathcal{A}$) and the resulting Ternary Decision Logic.
Sensitivity Analysis: Demonstrates how the metric responds to increasing Label Noise vs. Feature Noise, and confirms that the epsilon parameter successfully maintains metric robustness in noisy environments.
Developed and proposed by Kian Maleki.

Here is the proposed implementation for ambiguity_range_score:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.utils import check_consistent_length
from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve

def ambiguity_range_score(y_true, y_score, *, epsilon=0.0, pos_label=None):
    """Compute the Ambiguity Measure between perfect precision and recall.
    
    The Ambiguity Measure is the difference between the threshold required 
    for perfect precision and the threshold required for perfect recall.
    
    Parameters
    ----------
    y_true : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
        True binary labels.
    y_score : array-like of shape (n_samples,)
        Target scores, can either be probability estimates of the positive
        class or confidence values.
    epsilon : float, default=0.0
        The tolerance for "perfect" metrics. (e.g., 0.01 for 99% precision/recall).
    pos_label : int, float, bool or str, default=None
        The label of the positive class.

    Returns
    -------
    ambiguity : float
        The calculated range between thresholds. A smaller value indicates 
        better class separability.
    """
    check_consistent_length(y_true, y_score)
    
    # Calculate Precision-Recall curve and thresholds
    precision, recall, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(
        y_true, y_score, pos_label=pos_label
    )

    # 1. Upper Threshold: Minimum score where Precision >= 1 - epsilon
    target_p = 1.0 - epsilon
    p_indices = np.where(precision >= target_p)[0]
    
    # Clip index for thresholds
    t_upper = thresholds[p_indices[0]] if p_indices.size > 0 else np.max(y_score)

    # 2. Lower Threshold: Maximum score where Recall >= 1 - epsilon
    target_r = 1.0 - epsilon
    r_indices = np.where(recall >= target_r)[0]
    
    t_lower = thresholds[r_indices[-1]] if r_indices.size > 0 else np.min(y_score)

    # 3. Ambiguity Measure
    return float(t_upper - t_lower)

# Example Usage:
if __name__ == "__main__":
    y_true = np.array([0, 0, 1, 1])
    y_scores = np.array([0.1, 0.4, 0.35, 0.8])
    print(f"Ambiguity Measure: {ambiguity_range_score(y_true, y_scores)}")

title: PERF: Avoid unnecessary n_samples x n_samples diagonal sparse matrix in `_rescale_data`
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the workflow you want to enable
When fitting any linear model (e.g. LinearRegression, Ridge, ElasticNet) on sparse data
with sample_weight, the internal function _rescale_data is called to bake sample weights
into the data before solving. Currently it constructs an intermediate (n_samples x n_samples)
diagonal sparse matrix just to perform a simple row scaling, then runs a full sparse matrix
multiply through safe_sparse_dot.
For large sparse datasets this creates unnecessary memory allocation and computation on every
fit() call. The issue affects all linear models that support sample_weight with sparse input.
Describe your proposed solution
Replace the dia_array + safe_sparse_dot approach with a direct elementwise row-scaling via
csr_array.multiply(), which is built for this exact operation and needs no intermediate matrix.
Current code in sklearn/linear_model/_base.py:252:
if sp.issparse(X) or sp.issparse(y):
    sw_matrix = sparse.dia_array(
        (sample_weight_sqrt, 0), shape=(n_samples, n_samples)
    )

if sp.issparse(X):
    X = safe_sparse_dot(sw_matrix, X)

if sp.issparse(y):
    y = safe_sparse_dot(sw_matrix, y)
Proposed code:
if sp.issparse(X):
    X = X.multiply(sample_weight_sqrt[:, None])

if sp.issparse(y):
    sw = sample_weight_sqrt[:, None] if y.ndim > 1 else sample_weight_sqrt
    y = y.multiply(sw)
Both produce identical results — verified against the existing test_rescale_data test and
directly against the old implementation across all input combinations.
Why it is better:

Eliminates the (n_samples x n_samples) diagonal sparse matrix allocation entirely
csr_array.multiply(vector) is O(nnz) with no intermediate object;
dia_array @ csr_array constructs the diagonal object first, then runs a matrix-multiply
code path
For 100k samples: old code allocates a 100k-element data array and shape tuple for the
dia_array before touching X; new code works directly on the nnz non-zero entries

Describe alternatives you've considered

scipy.sparse.diags(sample_weight_sqrt) @ X — same problem, still builds an intermediate
diagonal sparse matrix
Keeping safe_sparse_dot — unnecessary here since .multiply() handles elementwise
scaling natively and always returns a sparse result

Additional context

Affected function: sklearn.linear_model._base._rescale_data (line 220)
Affected models: all linear models that accept sample_weight with sparse X —
LinearRegression, Ridge, ElasticNet, Lasso, and their CV variants
Tests: the existing test_rescale_data in sklearn/linear_model/tests/test_base.py
already covers sparse_container x n_targets combinations — no new test infrastructure needed
Fix is ready: branch perf/avoid-dia-array-in-rescale-data on fork

Describe the issue linked to the documentation
Today I felt like it would be nice to be able to see directly on https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.mixture.GaussianMixture.html#sklearn.mixture.GaussianMixture if it has array API support or not. Having to go to https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/array_api.html#support-for-array-api-compatible-inputs is possible but a bit tedious.
Until today I was thinking that we don't need this because "all estimators will support array API input, even if it doesn't make them faster". Which removes the need to explicitly list it on each estimator's page.
What do others think about this?

title: `partial_fit` for `Ridge`
body:
Describe the workflow you want to enable
The Ridge family is already compatible with the Array API, which is great for pytorch compatibility! It simplifies linear probing evaluations for foundation models.
However, these models often use datasets with many examples.
It is not always feasible to accumulate features in memory before passing them to a ridge classifier.
It would be nice if Ridge had a partial_fit method which allowed processing the dataset in batches.
With $D$ features and $N$ examples, Ridge would only accumulate the features statistics ($D \times D$) instead of all the features ($N \times D$)
Describe your proposed solution
We accumulate the sufficient statistics $A = X^\top X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D}$ and $B = X^\top Y \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times C}$, both of size independent of $N$. The closed-form ridge solution is $W = (A + \lambda I)^{-1} B$. Because $X$ is never materialized, memory is $O(D^2)$ instead of $O(ND)$, so the probe scales to arbitrarily large train sets.
Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant
Implement it outside of scikit learn: https://github.com/braindecode/OpenEEGBench/blob/ede655f1294feef15ff6be4d6e6d94628ab9187e/open_eeg_bench/ridge_probe.py#L79-L273
Then add a test for consistency with the scikit learn pipeline on a small random datasets: https://github.com/braindecode/OpenEEGBench/blob/ede655f1294feef15ff6be4d6e6d94628ab9187e/tests/test_ridge_probe.py#L42-L99
Additional context
We are using this for OpenEEGBench, a library for benchmarking EEG foundation models.
Context: braindecode/OpenEEGBench#32 (comment)

title: Make `_array_api_for_tests` accept a `dtype_name` and raise `SkipTest` if the requested dtype/device is not supported
body:
As discussed in #32460, the supported dtype can sometimes vary even if the device name is the same, and we need to do runtime inspection for instance using __array_namespace_info__.dtypes. It means that we would need to update all the array API test to pass both device and dtype_name to _array_api_for_tests to do this check and raise SkipTest when appropriate instead of running a test that will fail with a low level error message.
This is the case for PyTorch with the XPU device on different kinds of hardware: some Intel GPUs reachable via this device do support the xp.float64 dtype while others don't.
I think @cakedev0 has access to such hardware on his laptop.

title: Improve clarity of error message in validation utilities
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the issue linked to the documentation
Some error messages in sklearn.utils.validation are very brief and may not provide enough guidance to users.
For example, messages like "Input contains NaN" could be expanded to suggest possible fixes such as handling missing values before passing data to estimators.
I would like to improve the clarity of one such error message to make it more helpful for users.
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
Improve the wording of existing error messages in validation utilities to provide clearer guidance to users.
For example, instead of a short message like:
"Input contains NaN"
it could be expanded to:
"Input contains NaN values. Please handle missing values (e.g., imputation or removal) before passing data to the estimator."
This change would not affect functionality but would improve usability and reduce confusion for users encountering these errors.

title: Incorrect KMeans centers update
Add 'quantile' strategy to `calibration_curve`
body:
Describe the workflow you want to enable
Choose between different binning strategies ("uniform" fixed width bins, "quantile" equal mass bins) to estimate the calibration curve.
Describe your proposed solution
Adding in calibration_curve a new strategy = "uniform" or strategy = "quantile" option to switch between the two binning strategies. We can for now just add the option and change the default in a follow up PR.
We can also add (in the same or follow up PR) the strategy="isotonic"  option to implement the CORP approach as advocated in #23132.
Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant
No response
Additional context
There are multiple issues / PRs on implementing calibration metrics (for example the expected calibration error, the Brier score decomposition) and improving reliability diagrams:
#18268, #11096,  #22233, #21774, #23767,  #23132
There are two main ways to estimate the calibration curve (and metrics):

using binning, either "uniform" (fixed-width bins) or "quantile" (equal mass bins)
using isotonic regression, this is the CORP approach, see #23132

For the binning case, the quality of the estimate in the binning depends crucially on
1a. the number of bins, it seems that n_bins=n**(1/3) is best, this is tackled by #33856
1b. the binning strategy, it seems that "quantile" is better, see Roelofs et al or Nixon et al
Reading through the literature, I feel that the "best estimator for the calibration curve/metrics" is not yet settled.   Based on the experiments reported in the CORP paper, the isotonic regression seems the most accurate. However there are ways to debias the binned estimates for the Brier score decomposition that we could investigate, see Ferro and Fricker, 2012.
Also, we might want the different options with each its own benefits: fixed-width bins to visually compare different curves or put them in a dataframe, equal mass bins to get a more reliable curve with a manageable length (n_bins = n**(1/3)), isotonic regression for its accuracy but at the expense of  a crowded curve (length n).
Overall, having the different options seems to me the best way for further implementations of the calibration metrics or curve, without having to commit to one option over another.
cc @ogrisel @lorentzenchr

title: BUG _parallel_pairwise does not slice Y_norm_squared alongside Y when n_jobs > 1
body:
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
_parallel_pairwise chunks Y into slices for parallel execution but passes **kwds (including Y_norm_squared) unchanged. When euclidean_distances is called with Y_norm_squared and n_jobs > 1, this causes a ValueError due to shape mismatch between the sliced Y and the full Y_norm_squared.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import _parallel_pairwise, euclidean_distances
import numpy as np

X = np.random.RandomState(42).rand(13, 4)
Y_norm_squared = np.sum(X ** 2, axis=1)

# n_jobs=1: no chunking, Y_norm_squared matches Y — works fine
result = _parallel_pairwise(X, X, euclidean_distances, n_jobs=1, Y_norm_squared=Y_norm_squared)
print("n_jobs=1: OK", result.shape)

# n_jobs=2: Y chunked but Y_norm_squared stays full — crashes
_parallel_pairwise(X, X, euclidean_distances, n_jobs=2, Y_norm_squared=Y_norm_squared)
Expected Results
No error is thrown. The n_jobs=2 call returns the same distance matrix as n_jobs=1.
Actual Results
ValueError: Incompatible dimensions for Y of shape (6, 4) and Y_norm_squared of shape (13,).

title: BUG Spurious UserWarning with the deprecation of penalty in LogisticRegression
body:
When running this minimal example:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = make_classification(random_state=0)
log_reg = LogisticRegression(penalty=None).fit(X, y)
we get the following deprecation warning:
[/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py:1135](http://localhost:8888/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py#line=1134): FutureWarning: 'penalty' was deprecated in version 1.8 and will be removed in 1.10. To avoid this warning, leave 'penalty' set to its default value and use 'l1_ratio' or 'C' instead. Use l1_ratio=0 instead of penalty='l2', l1_ratio=1 instead of penalty='l1', and C=np.inf instead of penalty=None.

which is completely fine. In my case, I wanted an unpenalized model and thus fix C=np.inf:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import make_classification
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

X, y = make_classification(random_state=0)
log_reg = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf).fit(X, y)
and I get the following warning:
[/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py:1170](http://localhost:8888/Users/glemaitre/Documents/packages/python-stack/scikit-learn/scikit-learn/sklearn/linear_model/_logistic.py#line=1169): UserWarning: Setting penalty=None will ignore the C and l1_ratio parameters

I think that this warning is spurious. We probably set the penalty internally which trigger this warning.

title: ENH: Add confusion_matrix_diff to compare multiple models against a baseline
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

Describe the workflow you want to enable
When comparing classification models, users frequently need to understand how one model differs from another on a per-class basis. The current workflow requires manually computing separate confusion matrices and subtracting them:
cm1 = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred_baseline)
cm2 = confusion_matrix(y_true, y_pred_model2)
diff = cm2 - cm1

This pattern has no built-in support in sklearn and becomes error-prone when normalization is involved - normalizing before vs after subtraction gives different results and users may not be aware of this distinction.
There is also no standard scalable way to compare multiple models against a single baseline in one call.
Describe your proposed solution
Add confusion_matrix_diff to sklearn.metrics with the following signature:
def confusion_matrix_diff(
    y_true_or_cm_baseline,
    *args,
    precomputed=False,
    labels=None,
    sample_weight=None,
    normalize=None
)

Label mode (precomputed=False):
# Two models
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2)

# Three models
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2, y_pred3)

# With normalization
result = confusion_matrix_diff(y_true, y_pred_baseline, y_pred2, normalize='true')

Precomputed mode (precomputed=True):
result = confusion_matrix_diff(cm_baseline, cm2, cm3, precomputed=True)
Returns a 3D array of shape (n_comparisons, n_classes, n_classes) where:

Positive values = comparison model better than baseline
Negative values = baseline better than comparison model

The normalize parameter mirrors confusion_matrix exactly - normalization is applied to each matrix individually before subtraction, giving meaningful per-class rate differences rather than raw count differences.
Describe alternatives you've considered, if relevant
Users can subtract confusion matrices manually, but this does not handle:

Consistent normalization across matrices before subtraction
Multi-model comparison in a single call
Input validation for mismatched label sets or matrix shapes

A utility function makes this discoverable, correct by default, and consistent with the existing confusion_matrix API.
Additional context

No changes to existing functions — additions only
Placement: sklearn/metrics/_classification.py alongside confusion_matrix
Exported from sklearn.metrics
Full numpydoc docstring and tests included in the PR

Happy to adjust the API design based on maintainer feedback before writing any code.

title: DOC: Add explicit mathematical formula for biased standard deviation in StandardScaler
body:
Describe the issue linked to the documentation
The StandardScaler API reference says it Standardize features by removing the mean and scaling to unit variance and mentions numpy.std(ddof=0) in the "Notes" section, but does not explicitly state a mathematical equation.
For users with a statistical or mathematical background, it may be less transparent to rely on the documentation details of a third party library like NumPy than to provide a formal mathematical definition, which is easy to interpret as the difference between biased and unbiased estimators may not be immediately obvious to all users.
Suggest a potential alternative/fix
I propose adding the explicit LaTeX formulas for the $z$-score and the standard deviation to the "Notes" section of the StandardScaler docstring. This clarifies the use of the biased estimator (division by $n$) versus the unbiased estimator (also known as Bessel's correction, $n-1$), which might be a point of confusion for users.
I propose rewriting Notes as:
We use a biased estimator for the standard deviation, equivalent to numpy.std(x, ddof=0), that is:
.. math::
s = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^{n} (x_i - \mu)^2}

I’d be happy to submit a PR if this approach looks good.

title: Support for building against a SciPy which uses ILP64 BLAS and `cython_blas`
body:
Hi all, this issue is to propose adding support for building scikit-learn against a SciPy install that was built with ILP64 (i.e., 64-bit integers rather than the default LP64 / 32-bit integers - see https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/64-bit_computing#64-bit_data_models).
Context
SciPy has wanted to have solid/full ILP64  support for years (efforts going back to 2020, and feature requests before that), because there are use cases and algorithms where support for large arrays where array indices don't fit in plain int's is desirable. In the next SciPy release, 1.18.0, this will finally be arriving.
When building from source, there will actually be three builld modes:

LP64-only (default)
ILP64-only (opt-in with -Duse-ilp64=true)
ILP64 for all SciPy internals, but LP64 for linalg.blas and linalg.cython_blas low-level interfaces  (opt-in with -Duse-ilp64=true -Dcython-blas-abi=lp64)

See https://scipy.github.io/devdocs/building/blas_lapack.html#bit-integer-ilp64-blas-lapack for details.
Wheels on PyPI will continue to be LP64-only, so the ABI of cython_blas and cython_lapack won't be broken. However, when building from source, ILP64 can be chosen - and going ILP64-only means that downstream users of scipy.linalg.blas|lapack|cython_blas|cython_lapack need to work with that change.
Mode (3) can be useful as a transition mechanism for adopters (and wouldn't affect scikit-learn), but mode (2) is probably preferred.
Proposed solution
It is possible for scikit-learn and other downstream users to detect how SciPy was built, and adapt automatically - no new build flag will be needed in scikit-learn, it should "just work". Essentially, scipy.linalg.cython_blas will expose a blas_int that can be used. It's also not too difficult to use that conditionally when it exists, and fall back to plain int otherwise.
Then, there are two ways scikit-learn can go for its own Cython code:

Handle the change in sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pyx with a small shim in each function, and keep sklearn/utils/_cython_blas.pxd unchanged.
Change _cython_blas.pxd as well to use blas_int, meaning all consumers of that interface (~15 files currently) need to be adapted as well.

It's not an either/or. Option 1 is a very localized change, and should probably be done either way. Option 2 can always be done later - it has the benefit of actually enabling use of large arrays with scikit-learn APIs as well (option 1 doesn't, because _cython_blas.pxd still uses int). So it depends on whether there's a benefit in doing that.
Next step
I plan to open a PR for (1) soon. This is fairly well-tested now (https://github.com/rgommers/pixi-sklearn-ilp64), and we are adding a test package to SciPy CI that closely mirrors scikit-learn's _cython_blas wrappers. Also, we now have a regression test for Cython ABI/signature changes, so that should be fine now.
If you prefer to do (2), I'd be happy to work on that as well.

title: [BUG] BayesianRidge.predict with return_std=True fails to center test features, leading to incorrect predictive variance
body:
Describe the bug and give evidence about its user-facing impact
In BayesianRidge, the predictive variance calculation in the predict method is mathematically inconsistent with the training process when fit_intercept=True (the default). During fit(), the model centers the features (X - X_offset_), but during predict(), the variance is calculated using the raw test features X_test instead of centering them by the training mean X_offset_. As a result, the model reports its lowest uncertainty at the coordinate origin rather than at the center of the training data. For datasets far from the origin, this leads to significantly wrong uncertainty estimation, violating the principle that a Bayesian model should be most certain in the region where it has observed the most data.
Mathematical formulation
The original problem is $y = w^T x + b + \epsilon$. Instead, scikit-learn solves a centered version $y = w^T \tilde{x} + b' + \epsilon$, where $\tilde{x} = x - E[x]$, in order to find $w$ and $b'$, and finally $b$ is computed as $b = b' - w^T E[x]$. First, $b'$ is estimated using a frequentist approach (OLS/MLE) to be $b' = E[y]$, since $E[\tilde{x}] = 0$. This allows the problem to be reduced to $\tilde{y} = y - b' = w^T \tilde{x} + \epsilon$, on which a Bayesian approach is used to find $w$ (the posterior mean).
After $w$ is found, the predictive distribution of $\tilde{y}$ on a new test point $\tilde{x}$ is then given by
$$\tilde{\mu} = w^T \tilde{x}$$
$$\sigma^2 = \alpha^{-1} + \tilde{x}^T \Sigma_w \tilde{x}$$
But since $y = \tilde{y} + b'$, the predictive distribution of $y$ has the mean shifted to
$$\mu = w^T \tilde{x} + b'$$
while the variance stays the same.
However, our test point is actually $x$, so this all becomes
$$\mu = w^T (x - \mu_x) + b' = w^T x + b$$
$$\sigma^2 = \alpha^{-1} + (x - \mu_x)^T \Sigma_w (x - \mu_x)$$
where $\mu_x = E[x]$ (estimated using the training data).
Note that predict returns y_mean and y_std, where y_mean is exactly $\mu$, but y_std is not $\sigma$; instead it is
$$\alpha^{-1} + x^T \Sigma_w x$$
What is missing is to subtract $\mu_x$ from $x$ before the variance computation.
Steps/Code to Reproduce
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.linear_model import BayesianRidge

n = 4

x_train = np.linspace(80, 100, n)
y_train = x_train + 10*np.random.RandomState(0).standard_normal(n)
model = BayesianRidge().fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train)
x = np.linspace(-100, 100, 101)
y_mean, y_std = model.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1), return_std=True)
print(f"Std (x={x[50]:3g}): {y_std[50]:7.4f}")
print(f"Std (x={x[-1]:3g}): {y_std[-1]:7.4f}")
plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'r.')
plt.plot(x, y_mean, 'b-')
plt.fill_between(x, y_mean - y_std, y_mean + y_std, color='RoyalBlue')
plt.title('Actual Results')
plt.show()

x_train = np.linspace(80, 100, n)
x_train -= x_train.mean()
y_train = x_train + 10*np.random.RandomState(0).standard_normal(n)
model = BayesianRidge().fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train)
x = np.linspace(-100, 100, 101)
y_mean, y_std = model.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1), return_std=True)
print(f"Std (x={x[50]:3g}): {y_std[50]:7.4f}")
print(f"Std (x={x[-1]:3g}): {y_std[-1]:7.4f}")
plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'r.')
plt.plot(x, y_mean, 'b-')
plt.fill_between(x, y_mean - y_std, y_mean + y_std, color='RoyalBlue')
plt.title('Correct when data is already centered')
plt.show()

x_train = np.linspace(80, 100, n)
y_train = x_train + 10*np.random.RandomState(0).standard_normal(n)
model = BayesianRidge().fit(x_train.reshape(-1, 1), y_train)
x = np.linspace(-100, 100, 101)
y_mean = model.predict(x.reshape(-1, 1))
_, y_std = model.predict((x - model.X_offset_).reshape(-1, 1), return_std=True)
print(f"Std (x={x[50]:3g}): {y_std[50]:7.4f}")
print(f"Std (x={x[-1]:3g}): {y_std[-1]:7.4f}")
plt.plot(x_train, y_train, 'r.')
plt.plot(x, y_mean, 'b-')
plt.fill_between(x, y_mean - y_std, y_mean + y_std, color='RoyalBlue')
plt.title('Expected Results')
plt.show()
Expected Results
Lowest variance close to the training data.

Actual Results
Lowest variance close to the origin.

Note that this is fine if the data is already centered; this is the problem scikit-learn is actually solving.

    def predict(self, X, return_std=False):
        y_mean = self._decision_function(X)
        if not return_std:
            return y_mean
        else:
            X = X - self.X_offset_  # <-- just add this line
            sigmas_squared_data = (np.dot(X, self.sigma_) * X).sum(axis=1)
            y_std = np.sqrt(sigmas_squared_data + (1.0 / self.alpha_))
            return y_mean, y_std

title: TST: Add edge-case tests for StratifiedGroupKFold
body:
Current Problem
StratifiedGroupKFold has complex logic in _iter_test_indices and _find_best_fold.
There are several corner cases (e.g. groups with only one sample, very uneven class distributions, or small number of groups) that can lead to unexpected behavior or degenerate splits.
Current test coverage for these edge cases is limited.
Proposed Improvement
Add targeted tests in sklearn/model_selection/tests/test_split.py for:

Each group containing only one sample
One class appearing in only one group
shuffle=True with a small number of groups
Cases where n_splits is close to the number of groups

This will help prevent regressions and increase confidence in the implementation.

title: MAINT: Improve array API consistency in _validate_shuffle_split
body:
Current Problem
The helper function _validate_shuffle_split (used by train_test_split, ShuffleSplit, StratifiedShuffleSplit, etc.) still uses NumPy-specific patterns (np.asarray, .dtype.kind, etc.).
Other parts of the same file (StratifiedKFold, StratifiedShuffleSplit, etc.) have already been updated to support the Array API using get_namespace and move_to.
This creates inconsistency inside _split.py.
Why it matters
scikit-learn is actively improving Array API support across the library. Small inconsistencies make future maintenance harder and limit compatibility with non-NumPy arrays (such as CuPy).
Proposed Improvement
Make _validate_shuffle_split more consistent with the rest of the module by:

Using get_namespace where appropriate
Handling array API inputs gracefully while keeping the current NumPy behavior unchanged

Location:
sklearn/model_selection/_split.py → _validate_shuffle_split function
I have read the contributing guidelines and would like to work on this small maintenance task once the issue is triaged.

title: DOC: Modernize and improve examples in train_test_split
body:
Current Problem
The examples in train_test_split (sklearn/model_selection/_split.py) mix old NumPy-style output with pandas DataFrames, but the pandas part is not very clear or modern.
Many new users expect to see how the function behaves with DataFrames (column names and index are preserved, etc.).
Why it matters
train_test_split is one of the most commonly used functions in scikit-learn. Clear, modern examples help users understand the expected behavior, especially when working with pandas DataFrames.
Proposed Improvement

Update the pandas example to clearly show that column names and index are preserved in the output.
Add one short example demonstrating the stratify parameter.
Make the output more readable and consistent.

Location:
sklearn/model_selection/_split.py → train_test_split function (Examples section)
I have read the contributing guidelines and would like to work on this documentation improvement once the issue is triaged and approved.

title: DOC: Improve warnings and recommendations for LeaveOneOut and LeavePOut
body:
Current Problem
In LeaveOneOut and LeavePOut classes (sklearn/model_selection/_split.py), the documentation mentions that these methods "can be very costly" for large datasets, but the warning is quite vague.
Users often try these on datasets with thousands of samples and face very long runtimes or memory issues without clear guidance on when to avoid them.
Why it matters
New users frequently misuse LeaveOneOut() on large data, leading to poor experience. The current recommendation to use KFold or ShuffleSplit exists but is not prominent enough.
Proposed Improvement

Add a clearer UserWarning when n_samples is large (e.g., > 1000 for LeaveOneOut).
Improve the docstring with stronger recommendations and a short note about computational complexity.
Add a small example showing when to prefer KFold instead.

Location:
sklearn/model_selection/_split.py → class LeaveOneOut and class LeavePOut
I have read the contributing guidelines and would like to work on this documentation improvement once the issue is triaged and approved.
Is this suitable for a first-time contributor?

title: Add `MoveTo` transformer to move `X` to a different array namespace/device
body:
WarningThis issue is not yet ready for a PR. If you are interested in contributing to scikit-learn, please have a look at our contributing guidelines, and in particular the sections for new contributors and the "Needs triage" label.

This issue describes a new transformer MoveTo that can be used to move X to another array namespace and device. The goal of the transformer is to move the input array X to a specified array namespace (numpy, torch, cupy) and device (CPU, CUDA, MPS, etc). The transformer can not move y or sample_weight but that is Ok, because of #28668.
The goal is to enable a Pipeline like the following when using the experimental support for array API (and other use-cases where processing has to move from one namespace/device to another):
df = pd.read_parquet("data_file.parquet")
X = df[categorical_feature_names]  # categorical or str/object dtype
y = df[target_column_name]  # continuous value to regress.

pipeline = make_pipeline(
   TargetEncoder(),  # works on categorical X but also needs y, hence CPU for both
   MoveTo(namespace=torch, device="cuda:0"),
   Ridge(),  # only numerical inputs: faster to do it all on GPU, y follows X => y_pred on GPU.
)

cv_results = cross_validate(pipeline, X, y, scoring="r2")
Currently you can make the example above work by replacing MoveTo with FunctionTransformer(partial(torch.asarray, device="cuda:0")). However it is difficult for the average user to discover this particular FunctionTransformer incantation and looking towards the future where we want to offer a function that can "translate" a whole pipeline from running on one namespace/device to another (e.g. train on GPU, then deploy on CPU) having an explicitly named step that can be specially treated is useful.
xref #33444
